findings.title: Legacy global dispatcher not updated on fallback path
findings.body:
When the first `defineProperty` fails, the function returns before `legacyGlobalDispatcher` is set. Consumers that read the legacy symbol (Node's built-in fetch, older undici copies) keep using the previous dispatcher or none at all. The two globals now diverge with no error raised.

The symbols on `globalThis` exist so dispatchers are shared across undici instances. A module-local fallback breaks that contract, so other copies never see the new dispatcher.

Suggestion: Keep a fallback for the legacy wrapper as well and expose it wherever the legacy symbol is read. Alternatively, surface a warning or error so users know cross-instance sharing is unavailable.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Fallback dispatcher is shadowed by an existing frozen global value
findings.body:
`globalThis` is often frozen after a dispatcher is already installed under `Symbol.for('undici.globalDispatcher.1')`. That happens when this module ran earlier, when another undici copy set it, or when Node's bundled undici did. Freezing makes that property non-writable, so `defineProperty` throws `TypeError` and the new agent goes to `fallbackDispatcher`.

`getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`, and the existing non-nullish value always wins. The call therefore succeeds but has no effect, and the stale dispatcher keeps serving requests. If the new dispatcher was a ProxyAgent or carried TLS or connect restrictions, traffic silently bypasses them. Swallowing the error is worse than the old behavior, which threw loudly.

Suggestion: Track whether the fallback is active and prefer it over the global value. For example, set `let useFallback = false`, set `useFallback = true` in the catch, and in the getter use `return useFallback ? fallbackDispatcher : globalThis[globalDispatcher]`. Alternatively, keep throwing when the property already exists and cannot be changed.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Partial update leaves globals inconsistent
findings.body:
If the first `defineProperty` succeeds and the second throws `TypeError`, the error is swallowed. The comment claims "fallback storage is already set", but on this path it is not. The new dispatcher is published while the legacy dispatcher stays stale, with no signal to the caller.

Suggestion: Store `legacyAgent` in a fallback here, or roll back and treat both updates as one operation.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Stale dispatcher returned
findings.body:
Updates are silently lost if `globalThis` is frozen after the global dispatcher symbol already exists.

This happens in the common case: undici, or Node's bundled fetch, sets the dispatcher first, and the app calls `Object.freeze(globalThis)` later. Freezing makes the existing property non-writable, so a later `setGlobalDispatcher(newAgent)` fails in `defineProperty`. The `TypeError` is caught and `newAgent` goes into `fallbackDispatcher`.

However, `getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The global property is still the old agent, so the fallback is never read. The call appears to succeed but has no effect, and requests keep using the old agent.

Fix options:
- Have `getGlobalDispatcher` prefer `fallbackDispatcher` once it is set.
- Or clear `fallbackDispatcher` on a successful define and check it first.

findings.title: Swallowed cache-delete failure leaves revoked sessions usable
findings.body:
`delete()` removes the row from the DB, then deletes the cache entry. `cached_db` loads sessions from the cache first and only falls back to the DB on a miss. If the cache delete now fails silently, the full session payload (including auth data) stays in the cache until it expires.

This is not cosmetic. `delete()` is called by `flush()` on logout and by `cycle_key()` on login, which exists to prevent session fixation. When it fails, the old session key keeps authenticating for up to SESSION_COOKIE_AGE. Previously the exception surfaced (e.g. as a 500), so revocation never appeared to succeed when it hadn't.

Failed writes leave stale data, which is a lesser problem. Failed deletes defeat logout and invalidation, so treating both the same is not equivalent.

Suggestion: Keep raising on delete failures, or at minimum make it opt-in. Alternatively, on failure try a fallback invalidation, such as `self._cache.set(key, None, 0)` or a tombstone the loader treats as a miss-and-verify-with-DB. Also document clearly that a logged delete failure means the session may remain valid until cache expiry.

Suggestion: Apply the same mitigation as the sync path: propagate the error or invalidate the entry through a fallback.

Now logout looks successful while a copy of the session cookie can still authenticate until cache expiry. Swallowing errors is fine for `save()`, but for `delete()` it is a security trade-off. The database row is deleted first, then the cache entry. If the cache delete now fails (for example, a network error), the exception is only logged. `flush()`, `logout()` and `cycle_key()` all go through `delete()` and report success. findings.title: Deferral only guards the synchronous popup-open call
findings.body:
`_isOpeningOverflowPopup` is set only for the duration of `_overflowPopup.IsOpen = true`. The overflow ItemsControl can also realize containers later, for example:
- a later measure pass
- re-templating
- virtualization
- a secondary command becoming visible while the popup is already open

Any visibility change raised during those later realizations still calls `UpdateDynamicOverflow` directly. That clears and refills `_overflowItems` in the middle of the ItemsControl's realization, which is the same reentrancy that motivated this change. The guard should key off the ItemsControl's realization or layout, or the update should be posted to the dispatcher, rather than a narrow open window.

Suggestion: Consider deferring via `Dispatcher.UIThread.Post(UpdateDynamicOverflow, DispatcherPriority.Background)` with a coalescing flag whenever an update is requested while `_isDynamicUpdateInProgress` or while the overflow presenter is measuring, instead of only during `IsOpen = true`.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Deferred rebuild after open recreates overflow containers
findings.body:
`ApplyDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate` runs after the popup has opened and realized its items. `UpdateDynamicOverflow` then clears `_overflowItems` and re-adds every item. This can discard the containers just realized inside the open popup. Any state applied during popup opening may be lost, such as focus on the first overflow item for keyboard-opened menus (`_openedViaKeyboard`) or focus-visible classes. It also causes a visible double realization.

Suggestion: Diff the new overflow list against `_overflowItems` and apply only the minimal Insert/Remove operations, or re-apply keyboard focus after the deferred update.

findings.title: Deferred-update flag is left set if opening the popup throws

If `_overflowPopup.IsOpen = true` throws, `finally` resets `_isOpeningOverflowPopup` but `ApplyDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate()` is skipped. `_hasDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate` then stays true. findings.title: Race Condition
findings.body:
`Parallel.ForEach` updates the static `Dictionary` `TotalsByCustomer` from multiple threads with a read-modify-write. `Dictionary` is not thread-safe, so concurrent rows can lose updates, corrupt the dictionary, or throw. Any CSV large enough to run rows in parallel can trigger this, especially when several rows share a customer.

Related problems in the same method:
- `async void` means callers cannot await completion. Exceptions from a missing file, malformed rows (`cols[3]` out of range, `decimal.Parse`), or HTTP failures in `ToUsd` go unobserved or crash the process.
- `StreamReader` is never disposed, so the file handle leaks.
- Each parallel row makes a blocking HTTP call through `RateService.ToUsd`. It creates a new `HttpClient` per call and blocks with `.Result`, which risks socket exhaustion and thread-pool starvation.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Off-by-one
findings.body:
The loop condition `i <= start + size` returns `size + 1` items whenever enough items exist. For example, `Window(items, 0, 10)` returns 11 elements. Use `i < start + size`.

A negative `start` also throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` from the indexer. A negative `size` throws from the `List` constructor. Unlike `Page`, neither argument is validated.

notes: SQL injection: In `OrdersController.CountMatching`, `customerPrefix` is concatenated directly into the SQL text. An input like `x' OR 1=1; DROP TABLE orders; --` lets an attacker run arbitrary SQL. Use a parameter instead, for example `LIKE @prefix` with the value `prefix + "%"`, and escape LIKE wildcards if needed.

Sensitive information exposure: `src/Data/Db.cs` hardcodes the production SQL Server credentials (`User Id=shop_app;Password=Sh0p!Prod#2026`) in source. It also sets `TrustServerCertificate=True`, which disables certificate validation and enables MITM. The credential should be rotated and loaded from configuration or a secret store.

Insecure password reset token: `PasswordHasher.ResetToken` computes MD5 of `email + yyyyMMdd`, with no secret or randomness. Anyone who knows a user's email can compute that day's valid token and reset the password, which allows account takeover. Use a cryptographically random token (`RandomNumberGenerator`) stored server-side with an expiry and single use, or an HMAC with a server secret.

findings.title: Overflow Bypasses Cap
findings.body: `1 << attempt` overflows for large attempt counts, so the `d > 30` cap never applies. On 64-bit platforms, `attempt` = 63 yields a negative value and `attempt` >= 64 yields 0. A long-running retry loop that keeps incrementing `attempt` would then wait zero or a negative duration and spin without backoff. A negative `attempt` panics at runtime. Clamp `attempt` before shifting, for example by returning 30 when `attempt >= 5` and treating `attempt < 0` as 0.

The callers are not in this diff, so verify that every call site was updated for the new unit, or rename the function or return a `time.Duration` so the change can't be missed.

findings.title: Wrong Path/Types
findings.body:
Image/CSV diff regresses for renamed and copied files. The right-side blob is fetched from `rightCommit` using `diffFile.OldName` instead of `diffFile.Name`. That bug existed before, but these blobs now also drive image detection, `RightBlob`/`RightBlobSize`/`RightBlobMimeType` and the CSV diff.

Both branches are also gated on `Type` being `Add`, `Del` or `Change`. For `DiffFileRename` and `DiffFileCopy`, no blob is loaded at all. So `IsBlobTypeImage` is false and `LeftBlob`/`RightBlob` are nil.

Result:
- A renamed or copied image no longer shows the image diff.
- A renamed or copied CSV is diffed against nil blobs.

The old template looked up `$.BeforeCommit`/`$file.OldName` and `$.HeadCommit`/`$file.Name` regardless of type. Fix: use `diffFile.Name` for the right side, and include rename/copy types when loading blobs for render info.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Performance Regression
findings.body:
Every binary file in a diff is now streamed in full, on both sides, during each render. Previously `IsBin` files returned early, and content sniffing only read `SniffContentSize` bytes.

`getCommitFileBlobAndLimitedContent` calls `GetBlobLineCount`, which reads the entire blob just to count lines and bytes. The limit only caps what is buffered, not what is read. A PR or commit touching large binaries (e.g. archives, videos of hundreds of MB) will read all of that data on every diff page load.

For binaries, read only the sniff prefix and get the size from `blob.Size`, or by another cheap means.

findings.title: Use new file name for right blob
findings.body:
The right side (after commit) is looked up by `diffFile.OldName`. For renamed files this returns the wrong blob or none, which breaks `RightBlob`, its size, MIME type, image/CSV detection and highlighting. The old template correctly used `$file.Name` for the head commit, so use `diffFile.Name` here.

Improved code:
if (diffFile.Type == DiffFileAdd || diffFile.Type == DiffFileChange) && rightCommit != nil {
		c := getCommitFileBlobAndLimitedContent(ctx, gitRepo, rightCommit, diffFile.Name, contentLimit)

findings.title: Propagate line counts to render detail
findings.body:
`prepareDiffRenderDetail` stores the line counts only in the local variables `leftLineCount` and `rightLineCount`. It never copies them into `ret.leftLineCount` and `ret.rightLineCount`. As a result, `addTailSection` builds the tail section with `LeftIdx`/`RightIdx` set to 0, which breaks expanding the remaining lines. Assign the counts to `ret` before returning.

Improved code:
if leftLineCount <= lastLine.LeftIdx || rightLineCount <= lastLine.RightIdx {
		return ret
	}
	ret.needTailSection = true
	ret.leftLineCount, ret.rightLineCount = leftLineCount, rightLineCount
	return ret

A renamed (and possibly modified) image now gets empty `LeftBlobMimeType`/`RightBlobMimeType`, so `IsBlobTypeImage` is false and the image diff is no longer rendered. A renamed CSV gets nil blobs passed to `CreateCsvDiff`. In addition, the right blob is looked up with `diffFile.OldName` instead of `diffFile.Name`, which is wrong whenever the names differ. Load the left blob by `OldName` and the right blob by `Name`, and cover rename types too.

findings.body: For binary files the content limit is `SniffContentSize`. `getCommitFileBlobAndLimitedContent` still calls `GetBlobLineCount`, which streams the entire blob through `DataAsync` and counts newlines. The old code skipped binary files entirely. Diffs containing large binaries (archives, videos, large images) now read each full blob from git on both sides just to get the size, which can slow or time out the diff page. For binary files, get the size via a cheaper path and read only the sniff prefix.

findings.title: Errors Discarded
findings.body: `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseRead())` and `err = errors.Join(srvHalfCloser.CloseWrite())` do not include the existing `err`. This overwrites the `io.Copy` error and the client half-close error. Whenever `srv` is a HalfCloser, which is the normal case, copy failures such as "from backend to client" are lost, and `handleTCP` usually returns nil. Use `errors.Join(err, ...)` instead, as in the client branch.

findings.title: Possible Hang
findings.body:
`handleTCP` now waits for both copy goroutines before returning, so the deferred `srv.Close()` runs only after both finish. When one direction ends, only a half-close is propagated. The other `io.Copy` stays blocked until that peer closes its side.

If either conn is not a `nettype.HalfCloser`, nothing unblocks the second copy. This happens with a custom `Server.Dialer` returning a non-TCP conn, or with `connWithOneByte` wrapping a non-TCP conn, where the methods are silent no-ops. Previously the first finishing direction tore down both sides. Now the goroutines and connections can leak indefinitely, for example after a backend reset or full close while the client keeps its socket open.

Fall back to fully closing both conns when half-close is unsupported, or after an error in either direction.

findings.title: Possible Bug
findings.body: `io.Copy` errors do not unblock the other direction. Previously `return <-errc` returned on the first completion, and the deferred `srv.Close()` tore down both directions. If one direction fails (for example a reset, or a write error to a dead peer), the other direction's `io.Copy` stays blocked on a connection that nothing closes, so the SOCKS handler and its goroutines can hang until the peer closes. On the success path, half-close handles the shutdown. On the error path, the connections should be fully closed so the other copy unblocks.

Also, `readClosed` makes `Read` return `net.ErrClosed`, which `io.Copy` reports as an error even though a half-close is expected. It only matters when `CloseRead` is called while a `Read` is in progress.

findings.title: Response Body Leak
findings.body:
This callback returns `nil` error on a retryable status, so the pacer retries and overwrites `res`. The previous response body is never closed.

Retries now cover 500/502/503/504/509 instead of only 429. A run of transient server errors during downloads can therefore leak one body and connection per attempt.

Close or drain `res.Body` before returning `true`.

findings.title: Response body leak on retry
findings.body: In the `Open` download paths, a retryable status such as 502 or 503 returns `true, nil` without closing `res.Body` (or `downloadRes.Body`). Each retry overwrites the response, so the earlier body and its connection are leaked. Retries now fire for 500/502/503/504/509 as well as 429, so this is far more likely to happen. If retries are exhausted, the pacer returns a nil error, and the caller then treats the 5xx response as a successful download. Close the body before returning retry=true, and return an error carrying the status so exhausted retries fail.

findings.title: Set content length on retried uploads
findings.body:
`s.f.srv.Call` returns a non-error response for HTTP 4xx/5xx statuses only if the rest client treats them as errors. If `opts.ContentLength` is not set, a fresh `bytes.NewReader` body may be sent chunked, which breaks presigned S3 PUT uploads. Set `ContentLength` explicitly for each attempt so retries send a correct length.

Improved code:
body := chunk.Bytes()
opts.Body = bytes.NewReader(body)
contentLength := int64(len(body))
opts.ContentLength = &contentLength
uploadRes, err = s.f.srv.Call(ctx, &opts)
return shouldRetry(ctx, uploadRes, err)

findings.title: Hidden host capabilities
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` embeds `component.Host` as an interface, so only `GetExtensions` (plus the explicitly added `Report`/`RegisterZPages`) is promoted. Any other optional capability on the real service host is lost to extensions.

Extensions find these capabilities with type assertions, so they would now fail. Examples include `GetFactory` (`hostcapabilities.ComponentFactoryProvider`) and `GetModuleInfos` (`hostcapabilities.ModuleInfo`). Extensions that use them, such as an OpAMP-style extension reporting module info, would silently lose that functionality.

Fix: forward these interfaces too, the same way `RegisterZPages` is forwarded. Alternatively, build the wrapper dynamically so it preserves the underlying host's interfaces. Add tests asserting those capabilities still pass through.

findings.title: Datapath/userspace mismatch
findings.body:
The new ID-0 fallback lookup runs only when both the specific and aggregate lookups miss. It also has no counterpart in the Go `mapState.lookup`, which only considers the specific ID and `aggregateFor(key.Identity)`.

Today `aggregateFor` always returns 0, so this branch never runs and nothing changes. Once aggregates become non-zero, the verdict will depend on whether an unrelated specific entry exists:
- If an ID-0 entry is present (for example, one not expanded via `AllAggregates`) and no specific entry matches, the ID-0 entry is applied.
- If any lower-precedence specific entry exists, the same ID-0 entry is ignored, even a higher-precedence deny.

The userspace test `lookup` will not reflect either case. Either drop the fallback and rely on the expansion of ID 0 into `AllAggregates`, or apply the same precedence logic in both places.

findings.title: Non-promise thenables
findings.body:
On the fast path for a thenable chunk, `next()` returns whatever `chunk.then(...)` returns. Native promises return a promise, so they work. A spec-compliant custom thenable such as `{ then(res) { res(1) } }` returns `undefined` (or any non-promise value), so `next()` stops returning a promise. `for await` then fails with "Iterator result undefined is not an object".

The old async generator awaited any thenable correctly. A fix is to wrap the call, for example `new Promise((res, rej) => then.call(chunk, res, rej))`, or to resolve the value through a native promise before chaining.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Sync throw/hang
findings.body:
This affects both the `chunk.then` getter and the `then` call itself.

- **Fast path:** if either throws, `next()` throws synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise. `inFlight` has already been set to `true`, so every later `next()`/`return()`/`throw()` is queued forever and the stream is never finalized or destroyed.
- **Waiting path (`pump()`):** the same throw happens inside a `.then` callback. It becomes an unhandled rejection, and the caller's `next()` promise never settles.

The old generator caught this in its `try` block, which set the error and destroyed the stream. The throw should be caught and routed through `settleError`/`onChunkRejected`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Multi-settling thenable
findings.body:
In `pump()`, the callbacks passed to a custom thenable are not guarded against being called more than once, or calling both fulfil and reject. A misbehaving thenable could do either.

- Each call resets `inFlight = false` and calls `drain()`. If this happens while a later request is already in flight, the serialization invariant breaks: two pumps may run at once and overwrite the shared `callback`.
- A rejection may also `finalize()` the stream after a value was already delivered.

Native promises are unaffected. Guard the callbacks with a `settled` flag.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Null-byte check skipped
findings.body:
The fast path skips `validateArgumentNullCheck` because the real environment block cannot contain null bytes. `getEnvPairs()` uses the per-`Environment` store, though, and inside a Worker that is a `MapKVStore` (unless `SHARE_ENV` is used).

`MapKVStore::Set` keeps embedded NULs. So in a worker, `process.env.FOO = 'a\0b'` followed by `spawn(cmd)` now behaves differently:
- Before this PR, it threw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`.
- Now the value is passed through and silently truncated at the NUL when converted to a C string for `uv_spawn`.

A key containing a NUL is also silently dropped, because `Get(*key_utf8)` looks it up with a truncated `const char*`. The fix is to keep the null check for non-real stores, or to validate in `KVStore::Pairs`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Truncated key lookup
findings.body:
The default `KVStore::Pairs` looks up each key with `Get(*key_utf8)`, which takes a `const char*`. Any key with an embedded NUL (possible in `MapKVStore`) is therefore looked up under a truncated name. The result is either that the key is skipped, or that the value of a different key (the prefix) is emitted under the full key name.

Using the `Local<String>` `Get` overload, or a length-aware lookup, would avoid this mismatch.

findings.title: Behavior change
findings.body: The default path now ignores the JS-visible `process.env` and reads the native environment store instead. `process.env` is a writable property, so code that does `process.env = { ... }` previously had its replacement object inherited by `spawn()`, because the old code spread `process.env`. After this change the child silently gets the original native environment and ignores the replacement. I am not certain how much code relies on this, but it is an observable semantic change that the PR does not mention.

Keys and values are stored with their full length, so a null byte can be present. Previously `validateArgumentNullCheck` threw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`. Now the pair reaches `uv_spawn()` and is silently truncated at the null byte. Whether a worker can actually store such a value depends on `MapKVStore::Set`, which I did not see in this diff.

findings.title: Possible TypeError
findings.body:
The first condition uses optional chaining (`previous?.isCJ || next?.isCJ`), so either `previous` or `next` can be undefined. The second condition then reads `previous.kind` and `next.kind` without optional chaining.

This crashes when a whitespace node sits at the start or end of a sentence next to a CJ word. Example: a text node ending in `日本語\n` followed by an inline node such as emphasis or a link. Here `previous.isCJ` is true and `next` is undefined, so `next.kind` throws.

Use `previous?.kind` and `next?.kind`, or return early when either neighbor is missing.

findings.body:
The first condition uses optional chaining, so it treats `previous` or `next` as possibly undefined. The second condition then reads `.kind` on both without that guard. If a whitespace node sits at the start or end of a sentence next to a CJ character, this throws a `TypeError`. Use optional chaining here too.

Improved code:
!(
  (previous?.kind === KIND_K_LETTER && next?.kind === KIND_CJ_LETTER) ||
  (next?.kind === KIND_K_LETTER && previous?.kind === KIND_CJ_LETTER)
)

findings.title: Possible Crash
findings.body:
`isLineBreakAmbiguous` guards `previous` and `next` with `?.` in the first clause. The second clause then dereferences them unguarded (`previous.kind`, `next.kind`). If `previous` or `next` is undefined while the other side is CJ, this throws a `TypeError`. For example, a whitespace node at the edge of its parent with a CJ neighbor on the other side would trigger it. Guard these accesses with `?.`.

The function is also called before the `value === "\n"` check in `printWhitespace`. It therefore runs for every whitespace print (including plain spaces) under non-preserve `proseWrap`, so the crash is not limited to newlines. Evaluate `value === "\n"` first.

findings.title: Unguarded null trim
findings.body:
`trimHydrationBoundary` used to run only when a close marker was found (`if (close)`). It is now always called, and receives `null` when `claim.start` is missing or `locateClaimedEnd` finds no close. That happens when the boundary has no SSR range, for example on a hydration mismatch where the opening marker isn't found.

I can't see from the diff whether `trimHydrationBoundary(null)` is a no-op. If it treats `null` as "trim to the end of the parent", which is a common `cleanupHydrationTail` pattern, it could remove unrelated trailing SSR siblings.

Suggested fix: keep the guard, e.g. `const close = claim.start ? locateClaimedEnd(claim.start) : null; if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)`. A mismatch test where the slot has no SSR markers would confirm the behavior.

If mismatch handling later removes or replaces that close node, the cached `$fe` would be detached. `planReuseOwnClose` or the boundary trim would then use a node with no `parentNode`. The old code never read a cache here.

Uncertain: this depends on whether the mismatch paths can remove the close node while `$fe` is set. A mismatch test covering deferred revival inside a slot would settle it.

findings.title: Avoid cursor-based close lookup for slots
findings.body:
For slots, the old code used a close marker found by walking from the open marker. The new code uses `locateClaimedEnd`, which trusts the cursor whenever nothing is cached. While the slot boundary is still hydrating, the cursor may rest on a nested `]` close, so the wrong anchor can be reused. Use `locateSlotEndAnchor()` for slots, matching its documented contract of never reading off the cursor.

Improved code:
const close =
  frag.__vf & SLOT
    ? locateSlotEndAnchor()
    : frag.hydrationClaim && frag.hydrationClaim.start
      ? locateClaimedEnd(frag.hydrationClaim.start)
      : null

findings.body: For slot fragments, `planReuseOwnClose` now calls `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)`. The new `locateSlotEndAnchor` doc comment says the close must be located by walking from the open marker, "never read off the cursor", because slot content may still be under way. The old code used the eagerly located `currentSlotEndAnchor`. If this runs mid-hydration while the cursor rests on a nested or enclosing `]` close, the slot can reuse the wrong anchor. findings.title: Comma Path Splitting
findings.body:
The server splits the `paths` value on `,`, but commas are valid, unencoded characters in URL pathnames. `location.pathname` keeps commas as-is, for example `/tags/a,b` or `/products/1,2`. On the client, `paths.join(",")` turns `/tags/a,b` into the same string as the two paths `/tags/a` and `b`. The server then requests patches for the wrong paths, so the route is never discovered and the navigation 404s.

Previously, repeated `p` params handled these paths correctly. To fix this, encode each path before joining (for example with `encodeURIComponent`) and decode each entry after splitting. Alternatively, use a delimiter that cannot appear in a pathname.

findings.body: This has the same problem as the non-RSC handler. `pathParam.split(",")` breaks any requested pathname that contains a literal comma. Such a route will not match during lazy discovery. The client side in `rsc/browser.tsx` joins raw paths with `,`, so the server cannot tell separators apart from commas inside a path.

findings.title: Escape commas inside joined path values
findings.body:
URL pathnames can contain literal commas (for example `/a,b`), and the server splits on `,`, so such a path would be requested as `/a` and `b`. The route would then not be discovered correctly. Encode each path before joining so the delimiter is unambiguous, and decode each entry on the server. The integration test regexes would need updating to match the new encoding.

Improved code:
searchParams.set(
  "paths",
  paths
    .sort()
    .map((path) => encodeURIComponent(path))
    .join(","),
);
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Ambiguous path delimiter
findings.body: Paths are joined with `,` and split on `,` on the server. A URL path can legally contain a literal comma (for example `/a,b`, or a splat segment containing a comma). `URLSearchParams` percent-encodes the comma in the joined value, but the server decodes it back before splitting, so a single path `/a,b` is split into `/a` and `/b`. The server then returns patches for the wrong routes, and discovery of the real path can fail or return a false 404. The old repeated `p` params avoided this problem. Consider encoding each path with `encodeURIComponent` before joining and decoding after splitting, or document that commas are unsupported.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Backward compatibility
findings.body: The server now reads only `paths` and ignores `p`. During a deploy, or with a cached or stale client bundle still sending `?p=...`, `url.searchParams.has("paths")` is false and the server returns an empty patch set. This makes lazy route discovery silently fail for those clients, which then see 404s for valid routes. Falling back to `getAll("p")` when `paths` is absent would avoid this. If dropping `p` is intentional, the tradeoff should be called out.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Escape commas in paths before joining

The server then splits them into separate paths, so the manifest lookup will be wrong for those routes. Encode each path before joining and decode on the server (and in the RSC browser/server code) to keep the format unambiguous.

Improved code:
searchParams.set(
  "paths",
  paths
    .sort()
    .map((p) => encodeURIComponent(p))
    .join(","),

findings.title: Closing-tag regression
findings.body:
`_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` use `[^\S\n]+`, which requires at least one whitespace character after `{%`. The old lexer compared the stripped tag content, so `{% verbatim %}x{%endverbatim%}` and `{% comment %}x{%endcomment%}` both worked.

With this change, the raw-aware splitter never finds the closing tag. The rest of the template becomes a single text token, and the parser raises an "unclosed tag" `TemplateSyntaxError`.

The behavior is also inconsistent within the PR. The opening tag is detected after `strip()`, so `{%verbatim%}` and `{%comment%}` open a raw block. The named-verbatim end regex uses `[^\S\n]*`, so it accepts `{%endverbatim name%}`. Using `*` instead of `+` in these two regexes would restore the old behavior.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Inconsistent raw detection
findings.body:
`_raw_start_re` requires whitespace after `{%` (`\s+`), but `_raw_end_tag_re` strips the content and also treats `{%comment%}` and `{%verbatim%}` as raw openers. As a result, the same template tokenizes differently depending on whether some other `{% comment ...` or `{% verbatim ...` with a space appears elsewhere.

Example: `{%comment%}{{ x }}{%endcomment%}` works on the fast path when it is the only raw tag. If the template also contains `{% verbatim %}...{% endverbatim %}`, it goes through `_tag_re_split` instead. There the `{%comment%}` block enters raw mode and cannot be closed, because of the whitespace requirement in the end regex.

The fast-path check should accept optional whitespace (`\s*`) so it matches what `_raw_end_tag_re` accepts.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Allow closing tags without inner whitespace
findings.body:
The closing-tag regexes require at least one space after `{%`, so `{%endcomment%}` and `{%endverbatim%}` no longer close their blocks. Both were valid before, because the content is stripped and compared. Without a match, the rest of the template is swallowed as text and parsing fails with an unclosed-tag error. Use `*` instead of `+`, matching the named-verbatim regex.

Improved code:
_comment_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endcomment[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
_verbatim_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endverbatim[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Detect raw opening tags without whitespace
findings.body:
The fast-path detector requires whitespace after `{%`, so a template using `{%verbatim%}` takes the plain `tag_re.split` path. The verbatim handling was removed from `create_token`, so the verbatim content would then be tokenized and rendered as template syntax. This is a regression. Make the whitespace optional so that every opening tag recognized by `_raw_end_tag_re` (which strips the content) triggers the raw-aware splitter.

Improved code:
_raw_start_re = re.compile(
    r"%s\s*(?:comment|verbatim)\b" % re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START)
)
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Regression: no-space end tags
findings.body: `_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` require at least one whitespace character after `{%` (`[^\S\n]+`). `tag_re` and the parser still accept `{%endverbatim%}` and `{%endcomment%}`, and the old lexer matched them because it compared the stripped content. A template such as `{% verbatim %}x{%endverbatim%}y` now never finds the closing tag. The rest of the template is swallowed as text and the parser raises "Unclosed tag". The named-verbatim regex uses `[^\S\n]*`, so the three end-tag patterns are inconsistent. Using `*` in the unnamed patterns would fix this.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Allow zero whitespace in raw tag regexes
findings.body:
These patterns require at least one whitespace character after `{%`, so `{%verbatim%}` and `{%endverbatim%}` are not recognized. `_raw_start_re` skips the raw-aware path for `{%verbatim%}`, and `_verbatim_end_re` never closes on `{%endverbatim%}`. The old lexer accepted both spellings because it compared the stripped content. Allow zero or more whitespace characters so behavior matches the named-verbatim regex and the previous lexer.

Improved code:
_raw_start_re = re.compile(
    r"%s\s*(?:comment|verbatim)\b" % re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START)
)
_comment_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endcomment[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
_verbatim_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endverbatim[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Breaks async views
findings.body:
The new `wrapper` is always a plain sync function. When `non_atomic_requests` decorates an `async def` view, `iscoroutinefunction(wrapper)` returns False. Django's handler then treats the view as sync. It calls the view in a thread and gets back an un-awaited coroutine instead of an `HttpResponse`, so the request fails ("didn't return an HttpResponse object").

This is a regression, because the previous implementation returned the original view unchanged. When `iscoroutinefunction(view)` is true, the decorator should define an `async def` wrapper that awaits the view. Alternatively, it can mark the wrapper with `markcoroutinefunction`. Adding a test with an async view would catch this.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Async views broken
findings.body: The wrapper is a plain sync `def`, so `@non_atomic_requests` on an `async def` view now returns a function that `asyncio.iscoroutinefunction` reports as sync. Django's handlers will treat it as a sync view and call it in a thread. The call then returns an unawaited coroutine instead of an `HttpResponse`. Under ASGI this raises the "didn't return an HttpResponse ... unawaited coroutine" error. Before this PR the original function was returned unchanged, so async views kept working. The wrapper should be `async def` (awaiting the view) when the view is a coroutine function. Tests for the async case are also missing.

findings.title: Duplicate kwarg
findings.body:
`sort_keys=False` is passed explicitly, and `**self.options` is also passed. If a caller passes `sort_keys` to the serializer, the call raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Example: `serializers.serialize("yaml", qs, sort_keys=True)`.

Before this change, that option was forwarded to `yaml.dump` without error. It had no effect because of the dict representer, but it did not crash.

Use `self.options.setdefault("sort_keys", False)`, as is already done for `allow_unicode`. This keeps the default and also lets callers override it.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Avoid duplicate keyword argument TypeError
findings.body:
Passing `sort_keys=False` explicitly alongside `**self.options` raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'` whenever a caller supplies `sort_keys` to `serializers.serialize("yaml", ...)`. Before this change, that option was simply forwarded to `yaml.dump`, so this is a regression. Set the default with `setdefault`, as `allow_unicode` already does, so caller-supplied values are still honored.

Improved code:
def end_serialization(self):
    self.options.setdefault("allow_unicode", True)
    self.options.setdefault("sort_keys", False)
    yaml.dump(
        self.objects,
        self.stream,
        Dumper=DjangoSafeDumper,
        **self.options,
    )
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Possible Regression
findings.body: `sort_keys=False` is now passed explicitly alongside `**self.options`. A caller who passes `sort_keys` through serializer options, e.g. `serializers.serialize("yaml", qs, sort_keys=True)`, now gets `TypeError: yaml.dump() got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Previously the option was accepted, though it had no effect on dicts. This is a narrow edge case. Consider `self.options.setdefault("sort_keys", False)` before the call, or accept the break knowingly.

findings.body:
Passing `sort_keys=False` explicitly alongside `**self.options` raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'` if a caller supplies `sort_keys` in the serializer options. Use `setdefault` so that a user-provided value is respected and no duplicate keyword is passed.

findings.title: Behavior Regression
findings.body:
When no argument resolves to an existing path, the fallback now loads only `invocation_dir`. The old `_try_load_conftest(invocation_dir, ...)` also scanned its `test*` subdirectories. The glob is now applied only inside the `safe_exists(anchor)` branch, so the fallback no longer loads `invocation_dir/test*/conftest.py` early.

Trigger: all args are non-existent paths or long option-like strings (#10169, #11394), or `args` is empty. In these cases, conftests under `tests/` that register options or hooks are no longer loaded initially. This can produce "unrecognized arguments" errors for options defined there.

Fix: apply the `test*` subdirectory expansion to the fallback anchor too. For example, build the anchor list first, then expand each anchor with its `test*` subdirectories.

findings.title: Behavior Regression
findings.body: The old fallback called `_try_load_conftest(invocation_dir, ...)`, which also loaded conftests from the `test*` subdirectories of `invocation_dir`. The new fallback sets `anchors = [invocation_dir]` after the collection loop, so the `test*` expansion is skipped. When no existing path is found in `args` (for example a bare `pytest` run with no args and no testpaths), conftest files in `invocation_dir/test*/` are no longer loaded early. Those conftests' `pytest_addoption` hooks and other initial-conftest hooks would then be missed. The fix is to apply the `test*` expansion to the fallback anchor as well, for example by moving it into the final loop or a helper.

findings.title: Avoid unconditional plain-array output allocation
findings.body:
The array branch always writes into a freshly allocated plain `np.zeros` buffer, even when no endpoints are equal. This silently drops array subclasses and their extra state, such as masks or units, that the original `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` preserved, so `linspace` can behave differently for subclass inputs. Use the original subtraction unless some elements are actually equal, and use the `where=` path only in that case.

Improved code:
equal = start == stop
if equal.ndim == 0:
    delta = dt.type(0) if equal else np.subtract(
        stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
elif not equal.any():
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
else:
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal,
                        out=np.zeros(equal.shape, dtype=type(dt)))
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Subclass Regression
findings.body: For N-d inputs, `delta` is now written into a plain `np.zeros(...)` ndarray passed as `out=`. Previously `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` allocated its own output and could return an `ndarray` subclass (e.g. a unit-carrying or masked array) via `__array_wrap__`/`__array_ufunc__`. Passing a base-class `out` can drop that subclass type, units or mask from `delta`, and so from the `linspace` result for array-valued endpoints. The scalar branch has no such issue. It is uncertain whether any supported subclass is affected, since the diff does not show how `start`/`stop` are converted. A subclass test, or building `out` with `np.zeros_like`/`empty_like`-style subclass preservation, would settle it.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Normalization bypass
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the code that prepends `/` to relative patterns, and it only acts when the string already starts with `/`. A pattern that starts with a backslash skips normalization, then gets `/` prepended, which recreates the scheme-relative shape.

Example: the IIS rule `url="{R:1}"` with a capture of `\example.com` (or `\\example.com`) becomes `/\example.com`. Browsers treat that as `//example.com`, so the open redirect still works. The same applies to Apache rules like `RewriteRule /legacy/(.*) $1 [R=302]`.

Fix: normalize after the leading `/` is prepended, or make the helper also collapse a leading run that begins with `\`. Add test cases where the target has no leading `/` and the capture starts with `\`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Incomplete Normalization
findings.body: `CollapseLeadingSlashes` returns the input unchanged unless `url[0] == '/'`. The PR description says "any leading run of `/` and `\`" is collapsed, and the callers prepend `/` afterwards when the target doesn't start with `/`. A target such as `\\example.com` or `\/example.com` therefore passes through untouched, because it starts with `\`. The caller then prepends `/`, producing `/\\example.com` or `/\/example.com`. Browsers treat `\` as `/`, so this is again a scheme-relative off-origin redirect, which is exactly the open redirect this PR targets. Collapsing should also handle a leading `\` (and mixed runs), or run after the `/` prepend.

A pattern that doesn't start with `/` (for example `\example.com` or `\\example.com`) is normalized as a no-op and then gets `/` prepended. The result, `/\example.com` or `/\\example.com`, has a leading `/\` run and is emitted in `Location` when `PathBase` is empty. The same ordering applies in `RedirectRule.ApplyRule`, where the collapse also precedes the later `/` prepend. Normalize after the prepend, or make the helper handle a leading backslash. The new tests only cover targets that already begin with `/`, so they don't catch this.

findings.title: Stale Bounds check
findings.body:
The new "anchor at end" shortcut compares the current viewport end with `Bounds.Width`/`Bounds.Height`. During measure, `Bounds` still holds the previous arrange size, so the panel compares against the old extent.

Example scenario:
- The items source is replaced or grows a lot (say 100 → 1000 items) while the viewport sits at the old end.
- `_hasReachedEnd` is false at that point.
- `viewportEnd >= oldBounds` passes, so the anchor jumps to `itemCount - 1`.
- The scroll position snaps to the end of the new list instead of keeping the current offset.

The same stale comparison feeds `anchorAtEnd` in `RealizeElements`.

Uncertain: whether `_hasReachedEnd` is always still true in these reset or growth paths. If it is, the shortcut is skipped.

Possible fix: base the condition on the estimated or known extent for the current item count rather than the last arranged `Bounds`.

findings.title: Popup Can Go Off-Screen
findings.body:
In `Pointer` mode, once `_hasInitialPosition` is set, later size changes no longer reach the positioner. The positioner's constraint adjustments (flip/slide to stay inside screen bounds) are therefore never re-applied.

Scenario: a context flyout opens near the bottom or right screen edge, then its content grows (async items load, an expander opens). The popup keeps its original anchor and its new area extends off-screen.

The first arrange may also run before content reaches its final size. That locks in a position computed for a smaller popup.

Consider still repositioning when the new bounds would violate screen constraints, or re-running only the constraint adjustment with the original anchor point.

findings.title: Possible Panic
findings.body:
After the pidfd reports read-readiness, the code assumes `try_wait()` always returns `Some` and calls `.expect(...)`. If it returns `Ok(None)`, user code panics inside `Child::wait()`.

The readiness is not cleared and there is no retry, so any spurious readiness or wakeup before the child is reapable will panic. This includes readiness carried over after `reregister` into a new runtime.

Instead, clear the readiness when `try_wait()` returns `None` and keep polling, rather than panicking.

findings.title: Possible Bug
findings.body: `Pidfd::open` treats every `pidfd_open` failure as "no pidfd support" and returns `None`, and `PidfdReaper::new` then returns `Err((None, child))`, so the caller silently falls back to the signal reaper. That fallback is reasonable for ENOSYS, but `PIDFD_NONBLOCK` is only accepted by kernels 5.10+. On kernels 5.3-5.9, `pidfd_open` fails with EINVAL on every call. The `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT` cache is only set for ENOSYS, so each spawn repeats a failing syscall. This is only a performance cost. The cache could also cover EINVAL.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Panic Risk
findings.body: `poll` calls `.expect("pidfd is ready to read, the process should have exited")` on the result of `try_wait()`. A pidfd becomes readable when the process exits, so this is normally true. However, `Child` is publicly exposed and `try_wait`/`kill` go through `std_child()`. If a user calls `try_wait()` and reaps the child before the future is polled, the next `try_wait` in `poll` may return an error (ECHILD) or `Ok(None)`, and the `expect` panics. The semantics of the std `Child` also make `Ok(None)` possible under other conditions (e.g. spurious readiness). Returning an error or re-polling is safer than panicking.

The test `process_spawned_and_wait_in_different_runtime` covers this today, but the string-based coupling is fragile.

findings.title: Inverted Condition
findings.body:
The checks use `last_op_result().is_none()` on `fetch_build_data_queue` and `fetch_proc_macros_queue`. That is true only while the op has never completed, which contradicts the comment ("have finished fetching the build data once" / "finished loading the proc-macros once").

With the default config, where build scripts and proc-macro expansion are enabled:
- Before the first build-data or proc-macro load finishes, `fetch_semantic` is true. This is the case the PR is meant to prevent.
- Once each load has completed and `last_op_result()` becomes `Some`, `fetch_semantic` stays false. Semantic diagnostics are then permanently disabled for the session.

Both checks should be `last_op_result().is_some() && !op_in_progress()`.

findings.body:
The build-data and proc-macro checks are inverted. `last_op_result().is_none()` is true only before the first fetch has finished. Once build scripts or proc-macros load, `fetch_semantic` becomes `false` permanently, so semantic diagnostics are never computed again. The checks should instead require that a result exists, which matches the comment "have finished ... once".

findings.title: Fragile Error Matching
findings.body: `isResourceQuotaConflict` identifies retryable errors by matching two substrings in the error message. If the API server wording changes, or the error is wrapped or localized, the retry silently stops working and the original failure returns with no diagnostic. A structured check would be more robust, for example `StatusError.Status().Details.Kind == "resourcequotas"`. The `Details` field is populated for these conflicts, so it may be a better fit. The message match could stay as a fallback. This is a robustness concern rather than a confirmed bug, because the current message format is stable today.

findings.title: Stale dispatcher returned
findings.body:
Updates are silently lost if `globalThis` is frozen after the global dispatcher symbol already exists.

This happens in the common case: undici, or Node's bundled fetch, sets the dispatcher first, and the app calls `Object.freeze(globalThis)` later. Freezing makes the existing property non-writable, so a later `setGlobalDispatcher(newAgent)` fails in `defineProperty`. The `TypeError` is caught and `newAgent` goes into `fallbackDispatcher`.

However, `getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The global property is still the old agent, so the fallback is never read. The call appears to succeed but has no effect, and requests keep using the old agent.

Fix options:
- Have `getGlobalDispatcher` prefer `fallbackDispatcher` once it is set.
- Or clear `fallbackDispatcher` on a successful define and check it first.

findings.title: Stale Dispatcher
findings.body: If undici is loaded first and `globalThis` is frozen afterwards, `setGlobalDispatcher` silently stops working. This is the usual `Object.freeze(globalThis)` ordering. The existing `globalDispatcher` property becomes non-writable and non-configurable. Redefining it with a new value throws a `TypeError`, which the catch block swallows after storing the agent in `fallbackDispatcher`. `getGlobalDispatcher` then returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The old value is non-nullish, so the stale dispatcher is returned and the new one is never used, with no error. The fallback should take precedence once it has been set, or `getGlobalDispatcher` should check `fallbackDispatcher` first.

findings.title: Silent stale session
findings.body: `cached_db` reads from the cache before the database. If the cache delete fails, the DB row is gone but the cached session data stays valid until the cache entry expires. Before this change, the exception made `delete()` and `flush()` (used by `logout()`) fail visibly. Now logout looks successful while a copy of the session cookie can still authenticate until cache expiry. Swallowing errors is fine for `save()`, but for `delete()` it is a security trade-off. Consider documenting this explicitly, or retrying or invalidating the entry another way (e.g. setting a short-lived tombstone).

notes: Incomplete session invalidation: when the cache delete fails, the exception is now only logged. The session remains readable from the cache (which `cached_db` checks first) even though the database row was deleted. A logged-out or flushed session can therefore keep working until the cache entry expires, and the user is not shown any error. The stale cache entry also existed before this PR; the new part is that the failure is no longer surfaced to the caller.

notes: Stale session after failed cache delete: if `cache.delete()` fails, the session is removed from the DB but its cached copy remains. `load()` reads the cache first, so the session can stay valid after logout or flush until the cache entry expires. Previously the exception propagated and the failure was visible to the caller. Now it is only logged. This appears to be the intended trade-off for this ticket, so I flag it only as a behavioral note. Operators should monitor the new log message.

findings.title: Deferred update dropped
findings.body: `_hasDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate` is only consumed inside the `if (_overflowPopup != null)` block of the `IsOpen` handler. If an update is requested while `_isOpeningOverflowPopup` is true, the flag is set and then applied right after. It is never cleared or applied on other paths, so a stale flag could trigger an extra update later. This is low risk because the flag is only set while `_isOpeningOverflowPopup` is true, which only happens inside that block. The remaining uncertainty is whether setting `_overflowPopup.IsOpen = true` can throw. In that case the `finally` resets `_isOpeningOverflowPopup`, but the deferred flag stays set and is applied only on the next open.
